projectTitle: Fairmont Grain Co-op: The Data That Went Quiet During Harvest
projectTagline: A 20-video, start-to-finish build of a hybrid Azure/AWS grain-intake platform -- AKS, Terraform, and Azure SQL for one fictional co-op, from a single fragile on-prem server to a resilient, autoscaled system that survived its first live harvest, bug and all.
businessContext: Fairmont Grain Co-op runs four grain elevators, each instrumented for moisture, weight, and throughput, all landing on a single aging on-prem SQL Server with no offsite copy. During its six-week harvest window intake volume spikes eight to ten times the rest-of-year baseline -- exactly when that one fragile server was most likely to fail, and exactly when a lost season of settlement data would hurt the most. Dante Okafor, their Cloud Engineer, led the migration to a reliable, autoscaled cloud platform in time for it to carry a live harvest for the first time.
architectureSummary: The rebuilt platform runs grain-ingest on Azure Kubernetes Service, autoscaled by a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler and writing to Azure SQL, with an independent AWS failure domain for backup and Fairmont existing pricing data warehouse. All infrastructure is provisioned through Terraform across both clouds, with stored credentials replaced by Workload Identity Federation on Azure and an IAM instance-profile role on AWS. A FinOps and reliability dashboard watches cost against database load side by side -- the same dashboard that caught the series real incident, a NetworkPolicy label mismatch that silently blocked grain-ingest from the database until peak harvest traffic exposed it.

lessons.title: Meeting Fairmont Grain Co-op: Why the On-Prem Servers Can't Survive Harvest
lessons.summary: The discovery meeting: uncovering why Fairmont Grain Co-op's aging on-prem servers choke during harvest, have no real disaster recovery, and keep costing more every year -- before any migration gets designed.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Over the next 20 videos, you'll follow a real hybrid cloud migration end to end for a fictional regional agricultural cooperative, **Fairmont Grain Co-op** -- four grain elevators spread across the region, each wired with moisture, weight, and throughput sensors that report constantly during intake. All of that telemetry currently lands on a handful of aging servers in a closet at Fairmont's main elevator, and this video is the discovery meeting where you, Cloud Engineer **Dante Okafor**, sit down with the people who live with that system every day and find out exactly why it's about to fail again this harvest.

By the end of this series you'll have a containerized ingestion service on Azure Kubernetes Service, an Azure SQL database behind it, all of it provisioned as Terraform code, a zero-trust-style network lockdown, cost and reliability monitoring, and a hybrid tie-in to AWS -- and you'll have lived through a real incident during fall harvest that tests every piece of it. None of that gets designed in this video. This video is where the project always actually starts: in a room with two people who both agree something is broken, describing two different flavors of the same failure.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a lemonade stand that has exactly one cash register. Most of the year, one register is plenty -- maybe ten customers an hour. But on the one huge day of the town fair, three hundred people show up in a single afternoon, the register can't keep up, and it locks up right in the middle of the rush. There's no second register to switch to. And every year, the part that keeps breaking on that old register costs a little more to fix than it did the year before.

That's Fairmont Grain Co-op's computers. Most of the year, the sensors at the grain elevators don't send much data, and the old servers handle it fine. But during harvest -- the few weeks when every truck in the region is dumping grain and every sensor is reporting at once -- the servers choke. There's no second set of servers to fall back on if something breaks. And the company pays more every single year just to keep those same old, overloaded machines limping along.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the discovery phase of a cloud migration engagement, and the pattern here is one you'll see constantly in infrastructure work: the system isn't failing because anyone did anything wrong -- it's failing because it was sized for a company that no longer exists. Fairmont's on-prem stack was built years ago when the co-op ran two elevators with basic scale tickets. It now runs four elevators, each with moisture, weight, and throughput sensors firing readings continuously, and that growth happened gradually enough that nobody ever stopped to resize the platform underneath it.

In this meeting you'll hear the complaint from two different angles, and your job is to separate them before anyone sketches an architecture. Priya Nandankar, VP of Elevator Operations, is describing a **capacity and reliability** problem: during the six-week harvest window, concurrent load from all four elevators' sensors regularly saturates the single on-prem SQL Server instance, and telemetry either queues for minutes or drops outright -- exactly during the period when an inaccurate moisture reading can mean grain gets accepted at the wrong grade. Walt Keeler, Fairmont's IT Director, is describing a **cost and risk** problem one layer down: the servers running that database live in a single room at the main elevator with no replication and no offsite copy of anything, so a flood, a fire, or even a bad power event during harvest could mean losing the season's data outright, and the annual hardware refresh and support contracts to keep the aging boxes limping along get more expensive every budget cycle. Those are two different engineering problems wearing one complaint -- "the system can't keep up" -- and naming them separately here is what keeps the rest of this series honest.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write down what's actually true before the meeting

```
FAIRMONT GRAIN CO-OP -- BEFORE WALKING IN

Footprint:     4 grain elevators (Fairmont Main, Dellwood, Case Creek,
               North Junction), each with moisture, weight, and
               throughput sensors wired to a central data closet at
               Fairmont Main.
Current stack: 1 on-prem SQL Server box + 1 aging application server,
               both physically located in a single room at Fairmont
               Main. No secondary site, no cloud backup.
Seasonality:   Harvest runs roughly 6 weeks (mid-September through
               late October). During harvest, intake volume -- and
               sensor reporting volume -- is 8-10x the rest-of-year
               baseline.
```

## Step 2 -- Interview Operations and IT separately

```
PRIYA:  Every harvest, without fail, we get stretches -- usually
        right in the middle of peak intake -- where the readings on
        the dashboard just stop updating. Sometimes for a few
        minutes, sometimes longer. Our scale operators end up writing
        moisture readings on paper and keying them in later, by hand,
        because the system can't keep up with four elevators dumping
        data on it at once.

WALT:   The hardware in that closet is six years old. I budget more
        for keeping it alive every year -- we're on our third support
        contract renewal because the vendor keeps raising the price
        on parts that are getting harder to source. And if that room
        ever floods -- it's an old building, it's happened before,
        just not to that room yet -- we don't have a copy of any of
        this anywhere else. We'd lose the season.
```

## Step 3 -- Name the problems out loud, separately, in the room

```
YOU:    Priya, if we doubled the server's capacity tomorrow, would
        that also fix the risk of losing everything if that room
        floods?
PRIYA:  No -- that's completely separate. Faster hardware doesn't
        give us a copy somewhere else.
WALT:   Right, and even if we fixed the flood risk with a backup
        generator and a second room down the hall, that still
        wouldn't stop the dashboard from freezing during peak intake.
        Those are two different fixes.
```

## Step 4 -- Write the one-page current-state artifact

```
FAIRMONT GRAIN CO-OP -- CURRENT STATE AUDIT

Problem 1 (Operations, Priya):  Harvest-season reliability.
  Single on-prem SQL Server instance saturates under concurrent
  load from all 4 elevators during the ~6-week harvest window.
  Readings queue, drop, or require manual paper fallback at exactly
  the highest-stakes, highest-volume period of the year.

Problem 2 (IT, Walt):  No real disaster recovery.
  All infrastructure -- primary and only copy -- lives in a single
  physical room at Fairmont Main. No offsite replication, no cloud
  backup, no secondary region. A single building-level incident
  (flood, fire, extended power loss) during harvest could mean
  losing the season's telemetry outright.

Problem 3 (IT, Walt):  Rising operational cost.
  Hardware refresh and vendor support contracts for aging on-prem
  equipment increase every budget cycle, with no corresponding
  increase in capacity or reliability -- Fairmont is paying more
  each year for the same fragile system.

Agreement so far: these are THREE related but distinct problems.
None has been scoped yet -- that's Lesson 2 and Lesson 3.
```

## Step 5 -- Separate "broken" from "sized for a smaller company"

Nothing in this system is malfunctioning in the sense of having a bug. The on-prem SQL Server instance is doing exactly what a single, unreplicated on-prem box can do -- it just can't do that for a four-elevator co-op reporting sensor data in near-real time during an 8-10x seasonal spike. Writing that distinction down now is what keeps Lesson 2's scoping conversation from turning into "just buy a bigger server," which would re-create the same single-point-of-failure risk Walt just described, only with faster hardware.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Ran discovery with Operations (Priya Nandankar) and IT (Walt Keeler). Found three related but distinct problems: the single on-prem SQL Server instance saturates under concurrent load from all four elevators during the ~6-week harvest window; there is no offsite copy of anything, so a single building-level incident could mean losing a season's telemetry outright; and aging hardware/support contracts cost more every budget cycle with no capacity gain. These need to stay separated going into scoping -- capacity, disaster recovery, and cost are three different engineering problems, not one.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We met with Operations and IT and documented, in their own words, why the current system struggles every harvest and what it would actually cost the co-op to lose a season's data. These turned out to be three separate problems hiding behind one complaint, which is the most important thing to establish before any design work begins.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We now understand exactly why harvest season strains your systems every year, why there's real risk of losing a season's data outright, and why costs keep climbing without any improvement in reliability. These are three distinct gaps, not one vague 'the computers are old' problem -- and having them documented is what lets us fix all three correctly instead of just buying faster hardware and leaving the real risk in place.

lessons.title: Scoping the Migration: What's In, What's Out, What Waits
lessons.summary: Drawing a hard scope line around the harvest-telemetry migration -- containerized ingestion, infrastructure as code, and a real disaster-recovery path are in; a long list of adjacent asks gets logged and explicitly deferred.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 1 surfaced three real problems at Fairmont Grain Co-op: harvest-season reliability, missing disaster recovery, and rising cost. That's enough to understand the shape of the project -- but "migrate everything to the cloud" is not a scope, it's a direction. This video draws the hard boundary around what actually ships in v1: a containerized ingestion path for grain-elevator telemetry, running on Kubernetes, provisioned entirely as code, with a real cross-cloud backup target replacing the single-room, single-copy risk from Lesson 1.

Just as important as what's in scope is what gets named and explicitly deferred. A discovery meeting like Lesson 1's always surfaces more wishes than one migration should try to solve at once, and the discipline here is writing each one down with an honest reason, not just a shrug.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your family is moving to a new house, and everyone starts bringing boxes to the truck. Someone wants to bring the kitchen table, someone wants to bring last year's Halloween decorations, someone wants to bring a bike that doesn't even work anymore. If you just throw everything on one truck without deciding what actually needs to go today, you'll run out of room for the stuff that matters -- like the beds everyone needs to sleep in tonight.

So instead, you make a list: what has to move in on day one (the beds, the kitchen table), what can wait in storage for later (the decorations), and what maybe doesn't need to come at all (the broken bike). That's exactly what this video does for Fairmont's move to the cloud -- deciding what the new system absolutely has to handle first, and writing down, honestly, what's going to wait.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Scope discipline is what keeps a migration like this from quietly turning into a platform rebuild. The three problems from Lesson 1 all point to one structural fix: the sensor telemetry pipeline itself -- how moisture, weight, and throughput readings get captured, stored, and made durable -- needs to move off a single unreplicated on-prem box onto a platform that can scale during harvest and survive a building-level incident. That's the v1 boundary: a containerized ingestion service, an elastic compute layer underneath it, a managed database behind it, and infrastructure defined as code so the whole thing is reviewable and reproducible rather than hand-built the way the current system was.

Everything else that surfaces in a discovery process this broad -- and at Fairmont, plenty did -- gets an honest, individual disposition rather than a blanket yes or no. A predictive moisture-spoilage model, a farmer-facing mobile status app, migrating the co-op's separate accounting system, and a trader-facing real-time analytics dashboard all got mentioned in the same discovery week as the core telemetry problem. None of them are wrong ideas. None of them are also the problem Lesson 1 actually proved exists. Scoping them out by name, with a reason, is what keeps this migration from trying to solve five problems with the engineering budget and timeline for one -- and it's what gives Priya and Walt a clear, defensible answer when a sixth idea shows up mid-build.

```
PRIYA:  While you're in there anyway, could it also flag grain

```

The deferred items are the ones most likely to resurface as "but I thought that was included" mid-project if they're not acknowledged in writing now.

lessons.title: Defining Success: Harvest Uptime, Cost, and Recovery Targets
lessons.summary: Turning 'it needs to be reliable and cheaper' into written, testable numbers -- a harvest-season uptime target, a cost ceiling, and concrete RTO/RPO recovery objectives -- before any architecture gets drawn.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 2 drew a hard boundary around what ships: a containerized telemetry ingestion path, infrastructure as code, and a real cross-cloud disaster-recovery copy. That's a scope, not yet a target -- "make it reliable" and "make it cheaper" are not things you can design against or later prove you achieved. This video turns those two words into three written, testable numbers: an uptime target for the harvest window specifically, a cost ceiling the new platform has to stay under, and exact RTO/RPO figures for how fast the platform recovers from an outage and how much telemetry it's acceptable to lose in the process.

These three numbers are what every later architecture decision in this series gets measured against -- the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler's scaling thresholds, the Terraform remote-state design, the cross-cloud backup cadence, and eventually the real incident this project hits during fall harvest all trace back to the exact targets pinned down in this room.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you tell a friend "get here fast" for a party, with no actual time attached. One friend thinks fast means fifteen minutes, another thinks it means sometime before dinner. You'll both end up frustrated, and neither of you did anything wrong -- you just never agreed on an actual number.

That's the trap hiding inside "make the system reliable and keep costs down." It sounds obviously right, but nobody has said how many minutes of downtime during harvest is too many, how much money is actually too much to spend, or how fast the system needs to come back up if something breaks. This video is where Fairmont turns those fuzzy wishes into exact, written numbers specific enough that anyone could later check whether the new system actually hit them.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A target that sounds reasonable in a meeting and a target you can actually architect against are two different documents, and most infrastructure projects quietly miss expectations in that gap. The discipline is making every number falsifiable: given a specific outage on a specific day, there has to be an unambiguous answer for whether the system met the target or didn't. "Be reliable during harvest" is not implementable. "The telemetry ingestion path must maintain 99.9% availability during the harvest window, defined as no unplanned gap in sensor data longer than 5 minutes across more than one elevator simultaneously" is implementable, and Priya and Walt can each immediately agree or disagree with it.

The same precision has to apply to recovery, not just uptime, because Lesson 1's disaster-recovery gap is specifically about what happens *after* something fails, not just how often it fails. Two numbers matter here and they are not the same thing: **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)** -- how long the platform is allowed to be down before service is restored -- and **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)** -- how much data, measured in time, the platform is allowed to lose in a worst-case failure. For Fairmont, these land at an RTO of 15 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes during harvest: if the primary ingestion path fails outright, the platform must be serving telemetry again within 15 minutes, and whatever gets restored can be missing at most the last 5 minutes of readings, not the last hour, and certainly not the season. Pinning those numbers down now, with sign-off, is what makes the cross-cloud backup cadence in later lessons a design decision with a target, instead of a guess at "pretty often."
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Pull the testable claims out of Lessons 1 and 2

```
FROM THE AUDIT AND SCOPE:
  - "Reliable during harvest" was never defined in a percentage or
    a time window
  - "No real disaster recovery" implies a recovery target exists --
    but neither how fast nor how much data loss is tolerable has
    ever been written down
  - Rising cost was named as a problem, but no actual ceiling for
    the new platform's spend has been set
  - Harvest (mid-September through late October, ~6 weeks) is the
    period where all three numbers matter most -- the rest of the
    year has real but lower stakes
```

## Step 2 -- Draft the candidate targets and pressure-test them live

```
DRAFT TARGETS v1:
"During the harvest window, the telemetry ingestion path must
maintain 99.9% availability, with no unplanned gap in sensor data
longer than 5 minutes across more than one elevator simultaneously.
In a full outage of the primary ingestion path, the platform must be
restored within 15 minutes (RTO), losing no more than the prior 5
minutes of telemetry (RPO). Total monthly cloud infrastructure cost
must not exceed Fairmont's current on-prem hardware-refresh-and-
support run rate, measured over a full year to account for
seasonality."
```

```
WALT:   99.9% sounds abstract to me -- what does that actually mean
        in minutes, over six weeks?
YOU:    Over a 6-week harvest window, 99.9% availability allows
        roughly 60 minutes of unplanned downtime total, not per day.
        That's the number we're designing against.
PRIYA:  And the "more than one elevator simultaneously" part --
        why does that matter?
YOU:    Because one elevator having a brief local network hiccup is
        a very different severity than all four going dark at once.
        We want the system resilient enough that a single elevator's
        issue doesn't become a co-op-wide outage.
WALT:   15 minutes to recover and 5 minutes of data loss, worst
        case -- compared to today, where a bad outage could cost us
        the rest of the season. That's a real improvement I can
        explain to the board.
```

## Step 3 -- Write the targets with a concrete verification example

```
SUCCESS CRITERIA (v1):

Availability (harvest window, mid-Sept to late Oct):
  99.9% uptime for the telemetry ingestion path.
  No single-elevator gap longer than 5 minutes is itself a target
    breach; a gap affecting 2+ elevators simultaneously for any
    duration is treated as a severity-1 incident.

Recovery objectives:
  RTO: 15 minutes -- ingestion service restored and accepting
       telemetry again within 15 minutes of a full primary-path
       failure.
  RPO: 5 minutes -- at most the prior 5 minutes of telemetry may be
       unrecoverable in a worst-case failure.

Cost ceiling:
  Total monthly cloud spend, averaged over a full year, must not
  exceed current on-prem hardware-refresh-and-support run rate.
  Verified against Azure Cost Management budget data starting month
  1 of the live platform.

Verification example:
  Primary ingestion path fails completely at 2:00pm during peak
  harvest intake. Platform must be serving new telemetry again by
  2:15pm (RTO met). The last telemetry successfully durable before
  failure was at 1:56pm -- readings from 1:56pm to 2:00pm (4 minutes)
  are the acceptable worst-case loss (RPO met, under the 5-minute
  ceiling).
```

## Step 4 -- Review line by line, get an explicit yes from both stakeholders

Read the RTO/RPO distinction aloud specifically, since it's the one most likely to get nodded past: "RTO is how long you're down. RPO is how much you lose. They are not the same number and we are committing to both separately." Get an explicit yes on each of the three targets -- availability, recovery, and cost -- not a single nod to the whole document.

## Step 5 -- Version and date the targets

Save as `Fairmont_Success_Criteria_v1.md`, dated and signed by Priya and Walt. This document, alongside Lesson 2's scope statement, is what the hybrid Azure + AWS architecture in Lesson 4 is designed to satisfy -- not the other way around.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Converted 'reliable and cheaper' into three written targets: 99.9% availability during the 6-week harvest window (roughly 60 minutes total allowed downtime, with any multi-elevator simultaneous gap treated as severity-1), a 15-minute RTO and 5-minute RPO for full ingestion-path failures, and a monthly cloud cost ceiling pinned to the current on-prem run rate. These three numbers are the acceptance criteria for every architecture decision from Lesson 4 forward.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now have specific, numbers-based targets for uptime, recovery speed, data-loss tolerance, and cost, instead of open-ended goals like 'more reliable' and 'cheaper' that could never be proven met or missed. That gives us a concrete scorecard to design against and to report against once the platform is live.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've turned 'make it reliable and keep costs reasonable' into exact, agreed-upon numbers -- how much downtime is acceptable during harvest, how fast we recover from a failure, how much data we're willing to risk losing, and what the platform is allowed to cost. That's what lets us prove, not just claim, that this migration delivered what we said it would.

lessons.title: Choosing the Architecture: A Hybrid Azure and AWS Platform, Not a Single-Cloud Rebuild
lessons.summary: The first architecture decision: a hybrid Azure + AWS platform -- Azure running the containerized ingestion path and database, AWS holding the cross-cloud backup target and the co-op's existing data warehouse -- laid out before a single line of Terraform gets written.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With scope locked in Lesson 2 and three hard numbers to hit in Lesson 3, this is the first real architecture decision: which cloud, or clouds, this actually gets built on. The tempting shortcut is to treat this as a single-cloud rebuild -- pick one provider and move everything onto it. This video walks through why Fairmont's situation specifically calls for a **hybrid** platform instead: Microsoft Azure running the new containerized ingestion service and its database, and Amazon Web Services holding the cross-cloud disaster-recovery target that directly answers Lesson 1's "no offsite copy" risk, plus the co-op's existing AWS-hosted grain-pricing data warehouse that this platform needs to feed.

This decision is the architectural spine the rest of this series builds on. The AKS cluster running `grain-ingest`, the Azure SQL database it writes to, the Terraform modules provisioning both clouds, the zero-trust network lockdown pass, and eventually the real label-mismatch incident this project hits during fall harvest, all sit on top of the stack chosen in this lesson.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine your family keeps its savings in two different banks instead of just one. Part of the reason is safety -- if one bank's system goes down for a day, you can still get cash from the other one. But there's a second, simpler reason too: you already have a long-standing account at one of those banks from your job's direct deposit, and it would be silly to close it and move everything just because you're also opening a new account somewhere else for a different purpose.

That's exactly Fairmont's situation. The new grain-telemetry system is going to live mostly in one cloud, Microsoft Azure, because that's the best fit for the new containers and database it needs. But Fairmont also already has an account, so to speak, at a second cloud, Amazon Web Services, where its grain-pricing data warehouse has lived for years. Instead of forcing everything into one cloud and either rebuilding that existing system or leaving a dangerous single point of failure, Fairmont uses both -- Azure for the new work, and AWS for backup safety and the system that was already there.
lessons.explainProfessional:
A single-cloud rebuild would technically satisfy part of Lesson 3's targets, but it fails on two fronts specific to Fairmont. First, a disaster-recovery copy that lives inside the *same* cloud provider as the primary platform doesn't fully retire the risk Lesson 1 named -- a provider-wide regional incident, while rare, would put both the primary and its backup at risk simultaneously, which is exactly the single-point-of-failure pattern this migration exists to eliminate. Second, Fairmont already runs a grain-pricing data warehouse on AWS, built years ago for the trading desk, that the new platform's telemetry needs to eventually feed for elevator-level profitability reporting. Forcing that existing, working system onto Azure as part of this migration would violate Lesson 2's scope boundary -- the accounting/ERP-style "migrate everything" scope creep that was explicitly rejected.

The hybrid design instead gives each cloud exactly one job. **Azure** hosts the operational path: Azure Kubernetes Service runs `grain-ingest`, the containerized ingestion service, autoscaled via a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to absorb the harvest-season spikes Lesson 1 described; Azure SQL Database is the durable telemetry sink behind it; an Azure VNet provides the network boundary a later lesson locks down with a zero-trust-style `NetworkPolicy`. **AWS** hosts two things that are deliberately *not* the operational hot path: an S3 bucket serving as the cross-cloud backup target for Azure SQL's automated backups, satisfying Lesson 3's RTO/RPO targets with a genuinely independent failure domain rather than a same-provider replica; and continued access to the co-op's existing Redshift-based pricing data warehouse, which the new Gold-layer reporting work later in this series reads from rather than rebuilds. Every piece of both clouds gets provisioned through Terraform, with remote state held in an Azure Storage backend using blob-lease locking, so the infrastructure itself -- across both providers -- is reviewable, versioned, and reproducible rather than click-built the way the original on-prem system was.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- List the actual constraints before naming a provider

```
CONSTRAINTS:
  - A hard RTO of 15 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes (Lesson 3) -- the
    backup target cannot share a failure domain with the primary
  - Fairmont already runs a working grain-pricing data warehouse on
    AWS (Redshift) that this platform needs to feed, not replace
    (Lesson 2 explicitly rejected migrating unrelated systems)
  - Harvest-season autoscaling (Lesson 1, Lesson 3) needs a real
    container orchestration platform, not a fixed-size box
  - Walt's explicit ask: all infrastructure provisioned as code,
    reviewable, versioned -- across whichever cloud(s) are chosen
  - A real cost ceiling (Lesson 3) -- the design can't just be
    "use everything everywhere"
```

## Step 2 -- Assign one cloud, one job per responsibility

```
LAYER                  PROVIDER        RESPONSIBLE FOR              NOT RESPONSIBLE FOR
Container platform       Azure (AKS)     Running grain-ingest,        Long-term backup
                                          autoscaled via HPA           storage
Telemetry database       Azure SQL       Durable, queryable           Cross-cloud DR
                                          operational telemetry        independence
Cross-cloud DR target     AWS (S3)        Independent-failure-domain   Day-to-day
                                          backup copy of Azure SQL     operational reads
                                          backups, for RTO/RPO
Existing pricing          AWS (Redshift)  Grain-pricing/trading data   New operational
  data warehouse                         the co-op already relies on   telemetry
Infrastructure as code    Terraform,      Reviewable, repeatable       Business logic
                          state in Azure  provisioning across BOTH     itself
                          Storage w/      clouds
                          blob-lease lock
```

## Step 3 -- Name the alternatives seriously considered, and why each loses

```terraform
# Both providers are configured from day one, each scoped to its
# actual job -- this single file is the architectural decision made
# literal:

terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "fairmont-tfstate-rg"
    storage_account_name = "fairmonttfstate"
    container_name       = "tfstate"
    key                  = "platform.tfstate"
    use_azuread_auth     = true
  }
}

provider "azurerm" {
  features {}
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1" # backup target + existing data warehouse region
}
```

```
- Azure-only, with the DR backup living in a second Azure region:
  rejected as the FULL solution. It satisfies the letter of "have a
  backup" but keeps the entire platform inside one provider's control
  plane and billing/incident boundary -- a provider-wide event, while
  rare, would still threaten both copies at once.
- AWS-only, rebuilding the ingestion path on AWS and also migrating
  or re-platforming the existing Redshift warehouse: rejected. There
  is no technical reason to disturb a pricing data warehouse that
  already works, and doing so would violate the scope boundary set in
  Lesson 2.
- Keep everything on-prem, just add a second on-prem server room as
  the DR site: rejected. Still doesn't solve harvest-season capacity
  (Lesson 1), still requires Fairmont to own and refresh hardware
  forever (Lesson 1's rising-cost problem), and still shares a single
  organization's physical risk profile even across two rooms.
```

## Step 4 -- Write the one-paragraph justification you'll reuse later

```
"We're not forcing this onto one cloud just to keep things simple on
paper. Azure runs the new containerized ingestion service and
database because that's the right fit for the autoscaling and
networking this needs. AWS holds an independent backup copy -- in a
genuinely separate failure domain from Azure, which is what your
15-minute recovery target actually requires -- and keeps feeding your
existing pricing data warehouse, which already works and was never
in scope to rebuild. Two clouds, each doing exactly the job it's
best suited for."
```

## Step 5 -- Write down what this choice does NOT require

```
THIS DECISION DOES NOT REQUIRE:
  - Migrating or rebuilding the existing AWS Redshift pricing
    data warehouse
  - Any change to how scale operators or elevator staff do their
    jobs day to day
  - A single "rip and replace" cutover -- the on-prem system can keep
    running in parallel until the new platform is validated against
    the Lesson 3 targets
  - Managing two separate, disconnected sets of credentials and
    access policies by hand -- identity and networking across both
    clouds get provisioned as code, same as everything else
```

Naming what stays untouched is usually what turns a cautious stakeholder's "why do we suddenly need two cloud providers" into approval -- the real concern is almost never the provider count, it's the fear of disturbing something that already works.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Locked the architecture as hybrid: Azure Kubernetes Service runs grain-ingest (autoscaled via HPA) writing to Azure SQL, Terraform provisions both clouds with remote state in an Azure Storage backend using blob-lease locking, and AWS holds an independent-failure-domain backup target for Azure SQL plus continued access to the co-op's existing Redshift pricing warehouse. Single-cloud-Azure, single-cloud-AWS, and on-prem-plus-second-room alternatives were each considered and rejected for specific reasons tied to the Lesson 3 RTO/RPO targets and the Lesson 2 scope boundary.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We're not forcing this onto one cloud provider just to simplify the pitch. The new system and its backup genuinely need to sit in separate failure domains to hit the recovery targets we committed to, and the co-op's existing pricing system on AWS was never in scope to rebuild. Using the right cloud for each job gets us a more reliable result without expanding scope.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We're building the new system on the cloud platform best suited for it, and keeping your existing grain-pricing system exactly where it already works -- while using a second, independent cloud as a true backup, not a backup that could fail alongside the primary system in the same outage. That's what actually delivers on the recovery promises we made, not just the appearance of one.

lessons.title: Designing the Terraform Module Architecture: VNet, AKS, Azure SQL, and Remote State
lessons.summary: Whiteboarding the Terraform module boundaries for the network, the AKS cluster, and Azure SQL, plus a remote-state backend locked with Azure Storage blob leases -- before a single `terraform apply` runs.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The last video mapped the hybrid architecture Fairmont Grain Co-op is moving to -- `grain-ingest` running on AKS, writing to Azure SQL. None of that exists yet, and before Dante writes a single resource block, this video plans exactly how the Terraform code that builds it will be organized: three modules (`network`, `aks`, `sql`), what each one owns and exposes to the others, and a remote-state backend stored in Azure Storage, locked with a blob lease so two people -- or a person and a CI pipeline -- can never run `terraform apply` against the same state file at the same time.

Every name decided on this whiteboard -- the resource group, the module boundaries, the state storage account -- is what lesson 8 turns into real Azure resources, and what every later lesson in this series keeps reusing. Getting the module seams wrong here means refactoring live infrastructure later; getting them right means the AKS module and the SQL module can each change independently without the other needing to know why.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine you're building a recipe binder for a big family kitchen, and three different people need to use it at the same time -- one doing prep, one doing the stove, one doing dessert. You wouldn't hand everyone one single messy stack of index cards. You'd split the binder into three labeled tabs, and you'd put one lock on the binder itself so that if two people try to flip to a new page and scribble on it at the exact same moment, only one of them can write at a time -- the other has to wait their turn, so nobody's note gets half-overwritten.

That's exactly what we're planning here. The "tabs" are three Terraform modules -- one for the network, one for the Kubernetes cluster, one for the database. The "lock on the binder" is the remote state file, stored in Azure with a rule that only one person can be actively writing to it at once. We're deciding all of this on paper, before anyone picks up a pen.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is Terraform module design, and the discipline that matters is drawing clean ownership boundaries before any resource block exists, because a module boundary is far cheaper to get right on a whiteboard than to refactor out of live state later. We're splitting Fairmont Grain's infrastructure into three modules with a single responsibility each: **`network`** owns the VNet and its subnets, **`aks`** owns the AKS cluster and its node pool, and **`sql`** owns the Azure SQL logical server, database, and private endpoint. Each module takes in only the inputs it genuinely needs (the `aks` module needs the subnet ID the `network` module created, not the whole VNet resource) and exposes only the outputs the next module actually consumes -- that narrow contract is what lets the `sql` module's SKU change next quarter without anyone needing to touch `aks` at all.

The second decision is the state backend itself. We're using the `azurerm` backend, pointed at a storage account and container created once, outside of this Terraform configuration, specifically to hold state. The reason this matters operationally is Azure Blob Storage's native lease mechanism: when `terraform apply` or `terraform plan` starts, Terraform acquires a lease on the state blob, and any second `terraform` invocation against that same state -- a teammate's laptop, or a CI job that kicked off a few seconds later -- is refused the lease and fails loudly with a locking error, rather than both processes racing to write two different versions of the same state file. That's the actual mechanism that keeps a two-person team, or a human plus a CI pipeline, from corrupting Fairmont Grain's infrastructure state the first week two people touch it in the same afternoon.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Name the resource group and the module boundaries before writing a resource block

```
Resource group: rg-fairmontgrain-prod   (centralus)

MODULE    OWNS                                    DOES NOT OWN
network   VNet, subnets (AKS, data/private-endpoint) Compute, databases
aks       AKS cluster, system + ingest node pool    VNet, database
sql       SQL logical server, database, private      Compute, networking
          endpoint into the data subnet
```

## Step 2 -- Lay out the repository

```
infra/terraform/
  modules/
    network/
      main.tf        # azurerm_virtual_network, azurerm_subnet x2
      variables.tf
      outputs.tf     # aks_subnet_id, data_subnet_id
    aks/
      main.tf        # azurerm_kubernetes_cluster
      variables.tf   # takes aks_subnet_id as input
      outputs.tf     # cluster_id, kubelet_identity
    sql/
      main.tf        # azurerm_mssql_server, azurerm_mssql_database,
                      # azurerm_private_endpoint
      variables.tf   # takes data_subnet_id as input
      outputs.tf     # sql_server_fqdn, database_id
  envs/
    prod/
      main.tf         # wires the three modules together
      backend.tf
      variables.tf
      terraform.tfvars
```

## Step 3 -- Bootstrap the remote-state storage account on paper

```
State storage account: fairmonttfstate     (centralus, Standard_LRS)
Resource group:         fairmont-tfstate-rg
Container:              tfstate
State key:              platform.tfstate
```

This is the exact backend lesson 4 already locked in when the hybrid Azure/AWS architecture was chosen -- `fairmont-tfstate-rg` / `fairmonttfstate` / `tfstate` / `platform.tfstate`, with Azure AD auth rather than a storage account key. This storage account is deliberately created once, by hand or by a tiny one-time bootstrap script, outside of the Terraform configuration it will go on to store state for -- a Terraform config can't safely manage the very backend it depends on to run.

## Step 4 -- Write the backend block

```hcl
# infra/terraform/envs/prod/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "fairmont-tfstate-rg"
    storage_account_name = "fairmonttfstate"
    container_name        = "tfstate"
    key                   = "platform.tfstate"
    use_azuread_auth      = true
  }
}
```

The `azurerm` backend acquires a blob lease on `platform.tfstate` for the duration of every `plan` and `apply`. No extra configuration is needed to get locking -- it's a property of using this backend against Azure Blob Storage, not a separate feature to turn on.

## Step 5 -- Whiteboard each module's input/output contract

```hcl
# modules/network/outputs.tf
output "aks_subnet_id"  { value = azurerm_subnet.aks.id }
output "data_subnet_id" { value = azurerm_subnet.data.id }

# modules/aks/variables.tf
variable "subnet_id" {
  description = "Subnet the AKS node pool deploys into"
  type        = string
}

# modules/sql/variables.tf
variable "private_endpoint_subnet_id" {
  description = "Subnet the SQL private endpoint attaches to"
  type        = string
}
```

## Step 6 -- Wire the modules together in the environment root

```hcl
# infra/terraform/envs/prod/main.tf
module "network" {
  source              = "../../modules/network"
  resource_group_name = "rg-fairmontgrain-prod"
  location             = "centralus"
}

module "aks" {
  source    = "../../modules/aks"
  subnet_id = module.network.aks_subnet_id
}

module "sql" {
  source                      = "../../modules/sql"
  private_endpoint_subnet_id  = module.network.data_subnet_id
}
```

Nothing in `aks`'s module code ever reaches into `sql`'s resources, and nothing in `sql` reaches into `aks` -- the environment root is the only place that wires them together, which is exactly what lets either module be changed, tested, or even replaced on its own later.

## Step 7 -- Name the resources every later lesson will reuse

```
VNet:            vnet-fairmontgrain-prod        (10.20.0.0/16)
AKS subnet:      snet-aks-prod                  (10.20.1.0/24)
Data subnet:     snet-data-prod                  (10.20.2.0/24)
AKS cluster:     aks-fairmontgrain-prod
SQL server:       sql-fairmontgrain-prod
SQL database:     sqldb-grainingest
```

These exact names are what lesson 8's `terraform apply` creates, and what the Kubernetes and monitoring design in the next two lessons both build against.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Planned the Terraform module split before writing a resource block: network, aks, and sql as three independent modules with a narrow input/output contract, wired together only in the prod environment root. Remote state lives in fairmonttfstate/tfstate (platform.tfstate, the exact backend lesson 4 already named), locked natively via Azure Blob Storage's lease mechanism on every plan and apply -- no extra locking config needed with the azurerm backend.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned exactly how the infrastructure code for this project will be organized and how two people working on it at the same time can't accidentally overwrite each other's changes. That's the groundwork that lets us build the real cluster and database safely in the next few videos.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Before any cloud resources go up, we've planned how the underlying infrastructure code is organized and protected -- including a built-in safeguard that prevents two changes from colliding and corrupting the setup. This is the kind of groundwork that keeps a growing engineering team from stepping on each other later.

lessons.title: Planning the Kubernetes Platform: AKS, HPA Scaling, and a Zero-Trust NetworkPolicy
lessons.summary: Designing how grain-ingest runs on AKS -- the Helm-managed Deployment and HPA scaling strategy for harvest-season spikes, plus a deliberate, pod-level NetworkPolicy restricting Azure SQL access to exactly the ingest workload.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the Terraform module boundaries planned, this video designs what actually runs inside the AKS cluster those modules will create: the `grain-ingest` service itself, deployed and upgraded through a Helm chart, an HPA that scales it up for harvest-season traffic spikes, and a Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` that locks down which pods are even allowed to reach Azure SQL at the network layer. That NetworkPolicy is deliberately designed and applied as its own standalone control, owned by the platform/security side of the team and managed outside the `grain-ingest` Helm chart's own lifecycle -- a legitimate, common zero-trust pattern, not a shortcut.

This is the architecture every later lesson in this series builds on: the Deployment's pod labels, the HPA's scaling thresholds, and the NetworkPolicy's selector are all decided here, on paper, before a single `kubectl apply` runs against the real cluster lesson 8 provisions.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a factory floor with a records room that only certain workers are allowed into. The factory doesn't rely on workers just remembering the rule -- there's an actual badge reader on the door, and only badges with a specific color sticker open it. The person in charge of handing out badge colors is a completely different person from the shift supervisor who schedules who works which station that day. That's on purpose: the badge rule can be tightened or loosened by security without waiting on the scheduling office, and the schedule can change without security having to redo the badge rule.

That's exactly the plan for Fairmont Grain's new ingest service. The "badge rule" is a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that only lets pods wearing a specific label talk to the database. The "shift schedule" is the Helm chart that deploys and scales the ingest service itself. We're deliberately keeping those two things separate, each owned by the team that's actually responsible for it.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Two architecture decisions get locked down here. The first is the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler strategy for `grain-ingest`: scaling on CPU utilization with a 70% target, a floor of 3 replicas for normal harvest-adjacent traffic, and a ceiling of 15 replicas to absorb the real spikes several grain elevators generate simultaneously during peak intake. The HPA and the Deployment both live inside the same Helm chart (`charts/grain-ingest`), because they change together -- a resource-limit change almost always means revisiting the HPA target alongside it.

The second, more deliberate decision is the `NetworkPolicy`. Azure SQL access for the namespace is restricted at the pod network layer to only pods matching `app: ingest`, on top of whatever VNet- and firewall-level controls already exist -- a genuine defense-in-depth argument: even a pod that lands in the same namespace by mistake, or a misconfigured debug pod, has no network path to the database unless it carries that exact label. This policy is applied directly with `kubectl apply`, by the platform/security team, as its own artifact outside the `grain-ingest` Helm chart -- a decision made specifically so that a security-driven policy change doesn't have to wait on an application release train, and an application release doesn't have to carry security-review overhead for every deploy. The honest trade-off worth naming out loud at design time: the Deployment's pod labels and the NetworkPolicy's `podSelector` are now two independently-versioned pieces of configuration that have to agree with each other by convention, not by any single source of truth enforcing it -- a reasonable, common pattern, and one that simply requires both artifacts to be labeled consistently whenever either one changes.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Whiteboard the namespace and Helm chart contents

```
Namespace: grain-platform

charts/grain-ingest/
  templates/
    deployment.yaml   -- grain-ingest Deployment
    service.yaml       -- grain-ingest-svc (ClusterIP)
    hpa.yaml            -- grain-ingest-hpa
  values.yaml
  Chart.yaml
```

## Step 2 -- Design the Deployment's labels (the ones the NetworkPolicy will key off)

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
  namespace: grain-platform
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ingest
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ingest
        tier: ingestion
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: grain-ingest
          image: fairmontgrainacr.azurecr.io/grain-ingest:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
```

`app: ingest` is the exact label the NetworkPolicy in Step 4 is written against -- deciding both in the same planning session is what keeps them consistent at launch.

## Step 3 -- Design the HPA for harvest-season load

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest-hpa
  namespace: grain-platform
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: grain-ingest
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 15
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

```
REASONING:
  min 3   -- baseline covers normal, non-harvest intake traffic
  max 15  -- sized against last year's peak-harvest concurrent
             elevator submissions, with headroom
  70% CPU -- scales early enough that a burst doesn't outrun
             node-pool scheduling
```

## Step 4 -- Design the NetworkPolicy as its own standalone artifact

```yaml
# infra/k8s/network-policies/grain-ingest-db-access.yaml
# Applied directly via kubectl by the platform/security team --
# deliberately NOT part of the grain-ingest Helm chart.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest-db-access
  namespace: grain-platform
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ingest
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.20.2.0/24   # snet-data-prod -- SQL private endpoint
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 1433
```

```bash
kubectl apply -f infra/k8s/network-policies/grain-ingest-db-access.yaml
```

## Step 5 -- Write down why this lives outside the Helm chart, on purpose

```
OWNERSHIP SPLIT:
  grain-ingest Helm chart   -- app team, released on the app's cadence
  NetworkPolicy manifest    -- platform/security team, released on
                               its own cadence, reviewed as a security
                               control, not an app feature

BENEFIT:   a tightened network rule ships without waiting on an app
           release; an app release ships without a security review
           gate on every deploy.
CONVENTION REQUIRED:   both artifacts must agree on pod labels --
           there's no single source of truth enforcing that agreement,
           only the convention that whoever changes one checks the
           other.
```

## Step 6 -- Confirm the design against Fairmont Grain's zero-trust goal

```
GOAL (from the earlier network lockdown effort): even a pod that
lands in grain-platform without the app: ingest label -- a debug
pod, a misconfigured sidecar -- has no network path to Azure SQL,
regardless of namespace-level RBAC.

DESIGN CHECK: podSelector matches exactly the Deployment's pod
template labels (app: ingest) decided in Step 2. Both are reviewed
together in this same planning pass.
```

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Designed grain-ingest's HPA (3-15 replicas, 70% CPU target, sized against last harvest's peak concurrent elevator traffic) inside the Helm chart, and a separate NetworkPolicy restricting Azure SQL egress to pods labeled app: ingest, applied directly via kubectl by platform/security, deliberately outside the Helm chart's release cadence. Both artifacts key off the same app: ingest label today by design review, not by a single enforced source of truth.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We've planned how the ingest service will scale automatically during harvest, and how database access is locked down at the network level as its own independent security control. Keeping the security policy separate from the app's release process means a security tightening doesn't have to wait on an app deployment, or vice versa.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've designed the system so it scales itself automatically during your busiest harvest periods, and so the database is only reachable by the exact service that's supposed to reach it -- a zero-trust safeguard managed by the security side of the team, independent of day-to-day app releases.

lessons.title: Designing the FinOps and Reliability Dashboard: Budgets, Alerts, and Health Signals
lessons.summary: Planning an Azure Cost Management budget and alert, and a reliability dashboard that deliberately plots spend next to database load -- so a mismatch between the two is visible at a glance, not discovered by accident.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
AKS, the HPA scaling strategy, and the NetworkPolicy are all planned. This video plans the last piece of the architecture before implementation starts: how Fairmont Grain actually watches what this platform costs and whether it's healthy. We're designing an Azure Cost Management budget with alert thresholds, and a single reliability dashboard that puts cloud spend, AKS pod/replica counts, and Azure SQL load side by side on purpose -- so that if spend goes up for a reason that isn't matched by a real increase in database work, that mismatch is something a glance at one screen can catch, not something that only gets noticed after a customer complains.

This dashboard design is deliberate FinOps and reliability practice on its own merits: cost should track observable work, and the two signals belong next to each other precisely so a disagreement between them stands out immediately.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a thermostat that shows you both the temperature and how much electricity the furnace used today, on the exact same screen. If the furnace used way more electricity than usual, but the house isn't actually any warmer, that mismatch jumps out at you immediately, because both numbers are sitting right next to each other -- you don't have to go dig through two separate apps to even notice something's off.

That's exactly the dashboard we're planning for Fairmont Grain. One number is how much the cloud platform is costing. The other is how much real work the database is actually doing. We're deliberately putting them on the same screen, side by side, specifically so that if one goes up without the other, somebody notices right away instead of three weeks later on a bill.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Two pieces get designed here. The first is an Azure Cost Management budget, scoped to `rg-fairmontgrain-prod`, with a monthly amount and two notification thresholds (80% and 100% of budget) routed to an Action Group that reaches the on-call channel, not just an inbox nobody checks in real time. The second, more important piece is a reliability dashboard -- an Azure Monitor Workbook built on top of diagnostic settings flowing into a Log Analytics workspace -- with four panels chosen deliberately to sit on one screen: daily cost trend, AKS HPA current replica count against its ceiling, Azure SQL DTU utilization and active connection count, and `grain-ingest`'s own request/error rate.

The design principle behind putting cost and database load on the same panel set, rather than in two separate tools FinOps and SRE each check independently, is straightforward: a correctly-scaled system costs more precisely because it's doing more verifiable work, and those two curves should move together. If HPA correctly scales `grain-ingest` up -- replica count climbing, cost climbing right along with it -- but Azure SQL's connection count and DTU utilization stay flat or drop, that's not two unrelated facts, it's one dashboard showing a system that's spending more while doing measurably less of the thing it costs money to do. Designing the dashboard to make that kind of mismatch visible at a glance, rather than requiring someone to cross-reference a cost report against a separate database metrics blade, is the actual point of building one reliability dashboard instead of two disconnected ones.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Design the budget

```
Budget:       budget-fairmontgrain-prod
Scope:         rg-fairmontgrain-prod
Amount:        $18,000 / month
Time grain:     Monthly
Thresholds:     80% ($14,400) -- warning
               100% ($18,000) -- critical
Routed to:      ag-fairmontgrain-finops (Action Group)
```

```hcl
# infra/terraform/modules/finops/main.tf
resource "azurerm_consumption_budget_resource_group" "prod" {
  name              = "budget-fairmontgrain-prod"
  resource_group_id = data.azurerm_resource_group.prod.id
  amount             = 18000
  time_grain          = "Monthly"

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold       = 80
    operator         = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    contact_groups   = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.finops.id]
  }
  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold       = 100
    operator         = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    contact_groups   = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.finops.id]
  }
}
```

## Step 2 -- Design the Action Group so an alert actually reaches someone

```hcl
resource "azurerm_monitor_action_group" "finops" {
  name                = "ag-fairmontgrain-finops"
  resource_group_name = "rg-fairmontgrain-prod"
  short_name           = "finops"

  email_receiver {
    name           = "platform-oncall"
    email_address   = "platform-oncall@fairmontgrain.example"
  }
  webhook_receiver {
    name         = "teams-finops-channel"
    service_uri   = "https://fairmontgrain.webhook.office.com/..."
  }
}
```

## Step 3 -- Decide the four panels that go on one dashboard, and why

lessons.title: Provisioning the Core Infrastructure With Terraform
lessons.summary: Running the real terraform init/plan/apply workflow against the module design from lesson 5 -- standing up the resource group, VNet, AKS cluster, and Azure SQL server, with remote state locked by an Azure Storage blob lease.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Three videos of planning -- the Terraform module boundaries, the Kubernetes/HPA/NetworkPolicy design, and the FinOps/reliability dashboard design -- are done. This is the first lesson where any of it becomes real: bootstrapping the remote-state storage account, then running `terraform init`, `terraform plan`, and `terraform apply` for real against Fairmont Grain's Azure subscription, standing up `rg-fairmontgrain-prod`, the VNet and its two subnets, the `aks-fairmontgrain-prod` cluster, and the `sql-fairmontgrain-prod` server and database -- exactly the resources named on the whiteboard in lesson 5.

We also prove the remote-state locking mechanism actually works, not just that it's configured: running a second `terraform plan` against the same state while the first is still in flight, and watching Azure Blob Storage's lease mechanism refuse it. Nothing application-level goes in yet -- no Helm chart, no NetworkPolicy, no grain-ingest pod. That's deliberate: the infrastructure has to exist and be verified before anything is deployed on top of it, the same sequencing every other build in this catalog follows.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture pouring a concrete foundation and running the electrical wiring for a brand-new building, all from a single, precise set of blueprints -- the ones drawn up two videos ago. The construction crew doesn't eyeball anything; they follow the blueprint exactly, and before they pour a single thing, the site foreman double-checks the plan one more time. Then, to prove the site really does have a working "only one crew works here at a time" rule, two people try to grab the blueprint at once -- and the second one is told, correctly, to wait.

By the end of this video, the foundation, the wiring, and the building's basic shell are standing -- but it's still an empty building. Nobody's moved in the furniture yet. That's exactly right; the next phase of the project does that.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This is the first lesson where the Terraform plan from lesson 5 becomes billable Azure infrastructure. The sequencing matters: the remote-state storage account (`fairmonttfstate`) is bootstrapped first, by hand, outside the `prod` configuration, because a Terraform config can't manage the backend it depends on to even run. From there, `terraform init` downloads providers and connects to that backend, `terraform plan -out=tfplan` produces a reviewable plan against the module wiring from lesson 5 (network module, then aks module consuming its subnet output, then sql module consuming its own subnet output), and `terraform apply tfplan` -- applying the saved plan rather than re-planning at apply time -- is what actually creates the resource group, VNet, subnets, AKS cluster, and SQL server and database.

The detail worth being deliberate about, and worth demonstrating rather than just asserting, is the state lock. While the first `terraform apply` is in flight, Azure Blob Storage holds an active lease on `platform.tfstate`; starting a second `terraform plan` against that same state from another shell during that window fails immediately with a locking error identifying who holds the lease -- that failure is the mechanism working correctly, not a bug to route around. Once `apply` finishes, every resource gets verified independently with the Azure CLI rather than just trusting a clean `terraform apply` exit code, and the AKS cluster and SQL database are confirmed to exist with nothing running on either of them yet -- the Helm-deployed `grain-ingest` workload and its NetworkPolicy, both designed in lesson 6, get created in a later lesson, once there's a real cluster for `kubectl` to talk to.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Bootstrap the state storage account (one time, before touching the prod config)

This is the exact backend lesson 4 already named when the hybrid Azure/AWS architecture was chosen -- standing it up for real, for the first time, here.

```bash
az group create --name fairmont-tfstate-rg --location centralus

az storage account create \
  --name fairmonttfstate \
  --resource-group fairmont-tfstate-rg \
  --location centralus \
  --sku Standard_LRS \
  --encryption-services blob

az storage container create \
  --name tfstate \
  --account-name fairmonttfstate \
  --auth-mode login
```

## Step 2 -- Initialize Terraform against that backend

```bash
cd infra/terraform/envs/prod
terraform init
# Initializing the backend...
# Successfully configured the backend "azurerm"!
```

## Step 3 -- Plan, and read the plan before trusting it

```bash
terraform plan -out=tfplan
```

```
Plan: 9 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

  + module.network.azurerm_virtual_network.this
  + module.network.azurerm_subnet.aks
  + module.network.azurerm_subnet.data
  + module.aks.azurerm_kubernetes_cluster.this
  + module.sql.azurerm_mssql_server.this
  + module.sql.azurerm_mssql_database.this
  + module.sql.azurerm_private_endpoint.sql
  + azurerm_resource_group.prod
  + azurerm_log_analytics_workspace.prod
```

Nine resources, matching exactly the module boundaries whiteboarded in lesson 5 -- no surprise resource, and nothing from the lesson 6 Kubernetes/NetworkPolicy design, which is correct: Helm charts and NetworkPolicy manifests are applied with `kubectl`/`helm` against a running cluster, not created by this `terraform apply`.

## Step 4 -- Apply the saved plan

```bash
terraform apply tfplan
# ...
# Apply complete! Resources: 9 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
```

Applying the saved `tfplan` file, rather than running `terraform apply` fresh, guarantees the plan that gets approved is exactly the plan that gets executed -- nothing in Azure changed out from under it between the review in Step 3 and the apply here.

## Step 5 -- Prove the state lock actually works

While a second, deliberately slow change is applying in one terminal:

```bash
# terminal A
terraform apply
```

```bash
# terminal B, started seconds later
terraform plan
```

```
Error: Error acquiring the state lock

Error message: state blob is already locked
Lock Info:
  ID:        3f9a2c7e-....
  Operation: OperationTypeApply
  Who:       dante@fairmontgrain-build
  Created:   2026-10-29 14:02:11 UTC
```

This is the exact `platform.tfstate` blob named back in lesson 4 and bootstrapped in Step 1 of this lesson -- the lock being refused here is the payoff of that earlier naming decision, not a new mechanism introduced on the spot.

This is the Azure Blob Storage lease mechanism planned in lesson 5 working exactly as designed -- terminal B is correctly refused until terminal A's apply releases the lease, instead of the two processes racing against the same state file.

## Step 6 -- Verify every resource independently with the Azure CLI

```bash
az group show --name rg-fairmontgrain-prod --query "properties.provisioningState"
# "Succeeded"

az aks show --resource-group rg-fairmontgrain-prod \
  --name aks-fairmontgrain-prod --query "provisioningState"
# "Succeeded"

az sql db show --resource-group rg-fairmontgrain-prod \
  --server sql-fairmontgrain-prod --name sqldb-grainingest \
  --query "status"
# "Online"

az network vnet subnet list --resource-group rg-fairmontgrain-prod \
  --vnet-name vnet-fairmontgrain-prod --query "[].name" -o tsv
# snet-aks-prod
# snet-data-prod
```

## Step 7 -- Confirm the cluster is genuinely empty

```bash
az aks get-credentials --resource-group rg-fairmontgrain-prod \
  --name aks-fairmontgrain-prod

kubectl get namespaces
# default, kube-system, kube-node-lease, kube-public -- no grain-platform yet

kubectl get deployments --all-namespaces
# no user workloads
```

The infrastructure phase is done the moment these checks pass -- a real resource group, VNet, AKS cluster, and SQL database, all verified independently, with nothing deployed onto the cluster and no NetworkPolicy applied yet. The `grain-platform` namespace, the `grain-ingest` Helm release, and the NetworkPolicy designed in lesson 6 all get created in a later lesson, once there's a real cluster for them to land on.

Confirmed the Azure Blob Storage lease actually blocks a concurrent plan with a real locking error, then verified every resource independently via the Azure CLI. Cluster is live and confirmed empty -- no grain-platform namespace, no workloads yet.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The real cloud infrastructure for this project is now live -- network, Kubernetes cluster, and database are all provisioned and independently verified, built exactly from the plan we reviewed in earlier videos. We also confirmed the safety mechanism that prevents two people from making conflicting changes at once actually works, not just that it's configured. Nothing runs on the infrastructure yet, which is expected -- that's the next phase.
workplaceExplanation.executive: The technical foundation for the new system is now physically running in Azure -- the network, the compute cluster, and the database are all provisioned and verified working, including a built-in safeguard against two changes colliding.
