lessons.title: Containerizing grain-ingest and Deploying to AKS with Helm
lessons.summary: Dante Okafor writes the Dockerfile for Fairmont's grain-ingest service, packages it as a Helm chart with an HPA, and deploys it onto the AKS cluster Terraform provisioned in Lesson 8 -- the Deployment's pod labels are the exact label a later lesson's security pass will quietly fail to match.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
With the AKS cluster, Azure SQL instance, and Terraform-managed networking from Lesson 8 now standing, Dante Okafor has a cluster with nothing running on it. This lesson builds the thing that actually does Fairmont Grain Co-op's work: `grain-ingest`, the Python service that receives scale-house and elevator-leg weight readings during harvest and writes them into Azure SQL. Dante writes a production Dockerfile, packages the Deployment, Service, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler into a Helm chart (rather than raw manifests, so the same chart can be promoted from dev to staging to the real harvest-season cluster), and runs the first `helm install`.

This lesson is scoped to getting grain-ingest running and able to scale under load. Locking down who's allowed to reach the database at the network layer, hardening credentials, and routine operational automation are separate lessons immediately ahead -- this one just gets the workload itself deployed and autoscaling correctly.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about setting up a brand-new grain scale house right before harvest. First you need actual scale operators standing at the window, not just an empty building. This lesson is Dante hiring that first crew and writing down exactly how they're identified on their name badges -- say, 'Ingest Crew' -- and setting a rule that says: when trucks are lined up out the door during harvest, automatically call in more people wearing that same badge, and send them home again once the line is short.

That name on the badge matters more than it sounds like it should. Every other rule anyone writes about this crew later -- who's allowed through which doors, who gets which keys -- is going to be written by checking that exact badge name. Get it right now, and it just works. Get it even slightly wrong later, and a door that's supposed to open for this crew simply won't, and nobody will notice until the line gets long.
lessons.explainProfessional:
grain-ingest is a Python service (using `pyodbc` against Azure SQL) that Fairmont's scale houses and elevator legs post weight-ticket events to continuously during harvest, and lightly the rest of the year -- exactly the bursty load profile a HorizontalPodAutoscaler is built for. Dante writes a multi-stage Dockerfile (a `python:3.12-slim` build stage resolving dependencies into a virtualenv, copied into an equally slim non-root runtime stage) and wraps the Deployment, Service, and HPA in a Helm chart under `charts/grain-ingest/`, parameterized by `values.yaml` so the same chart deploys to `dev`, `staging`, and the production AKS cluster with only replica counts and resource requests changing between them.

The one decision worth naming carefully here is the pod label. Helm's own chart convention generates a label from the release and chart name, and Dante keeps it simple and literal: every pod the Deployment creates carries `app: grain-ingest`, and the Deployment's `selector.matchLabels` matches that exact string. It's an unremarkable, idiomatic choice -- there's nothing unusual or careless about it. It's also, as it happens, the only place in this entire implementation phase where that label gets defined from scratch; every later lesson that needs to select these pods is reading this one. The HPA targets 70% average CPU utilization across the Deployment, with `minReplicas: 3` (enough to survive a pod eviction without dropping a weigh-in) and `maxReplicas: 20` (sized against Lesson 8's node pool), and Dante validates the first rollout and a manual scale-up before moving on.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Write the Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# ---- build stage ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN python -m venv /opt/venv \
  && /opt/venv/bin/pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .

# ---- runtime stage ----
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash ingest
COPY --from=build /opt/venv /opt/venv
COPY --from=build /app /app
ENV PATH="/opt/venv/bin:$PATH"
USER ingest
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 \
  CMD python -c "import urllib.request; urllib.request.urlopen('http://localhost:8080/healthz')" || exit 1
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8080"]
```

## Step 2 -- Scaffold the Helm chart

```
charts/grain-ingest/
  Chart.yaml
  values.yaml
  templates/
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    hpa.yaml
```

## Step 3 -- Write the Deployment template -- the label that matters

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
  namespace: fairmont
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: grain-ingest
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: grain-ingest
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: grain-ingest
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              cpu: 500m
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
```

Every pod this Deployment ever creates carries exactly one label for identity: `app: grain-ingest`, in both the selector and the pod template. That's the string every later lesson needs to repeat exactly if it wants to target these pods.

## Step 4 -- Write the Service

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
  namespace: fairmont
spec:
  selector:
    app: grain-ingest
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
```

## Step 5 -- Write the HorizontalPodAutoscaler

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
  namespace: fairmont
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: grain-ingest
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 20
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70
```

## Step 6 -- Install and verify

```bash
helm upgrade --install grain-ingest ./charts/grain-ingest \
  --namespace fairmont --create-namespace \
  -f values-prod.yaml

kubectl get pods -n fairmont -l app=grain-ingest
kubectl get hpa grain-ingest -n fairmont
```

Dante confirms three pods come up healthy, each carrying `app: grain-ingest`, and forces a short synthetic load test to watch the HPA scale out to six replicas and back down -- the autoscaling behaves exactly as designed before harvest ever puts real load on it.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Containerized grain-ingest with a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile and deployed it via a parameterized Helm chart -- Deployment, Service, and HPA (min 3 / 70% CPU target / max 20) -- onto the Lesson 8 AKS cluster. Pod identity is the single label `app: grain-ingest`, set in both selector.matchLabels and the pod template, which every later network and ops lesson reads rather than redefines.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: The ingestion service is now actually running on the new cluster and can automatically add capacity during a harvest rush and scale back down afterward. This is the foundation everything else -- security, access control, monitoring -- gets layered onto next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Fairmont's scale-house data now flows through the new cloud platform we built, and it can automatically handle harvest's traffic spikes without anyone manually adding servers. This is the first real workload running on the new foundation.

lessons.title: Locking Down Database Access with a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy
lessons.summary: A fast, reasonable-sounding security pass: Dante applies a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy restricting which pods can reach Azure SQL, directly via kubectl rather than through the Helm chart -- and its podSelector quietly doesn't match the Deployment label Lesson 9 actually shipped.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
grain-ingest is running, but at this point in Fairmont's build, nothing inside the `fairmont` namespace actually stops some other pod -- a debugging shell, a future service, anything -- from opening a connection straight to Azure SQL. A pre-harvest security review flags this as an easy, overdue fix, and Dante closes it the same week: a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy that permits egress to the database only from pods carrying the ingestion service's label.

With the harvest security window closing and the Helm chart's own review queue backed up a day, Dante applies the policy directly with `kubectl apply -f`, planning to fold it into the chart properly once things calm down. He writes it, tests that the policy's allow/deny logic works correctly, and ships it. The fix is real, the testing is real, and the policy does exactly what it was written to do -- which is a different question from whether it was written against the right label.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture adding a locked door in front of the one hallway that leads to the company's filing cabinets, with a card reader that only lets through people wearing a badge that says 'Dock Crew.' You test the door by walking up wearing a badge you printed yourself that says 'Dock Crew,' and sure enough, it opens. Great -- the door works.

But the actual dock crew walking around the building that week is wearing a different badge -- one that says 'Grain Ingest Crew,' because that's what got printed for them last week. Nobody checked whether the two badges said the same words. The door isn't broken. It's doing exactly what it was told. It's just been told to look for a badge that doesn't match the one anybody is actually wearing.
lessons.explainProfessional:
Dante writes two NetworkPolicy objects in the `fairmont` namespace: a default-deny baseline for all egress, and a narrow allow rule permitting egress to Azure SQL's private endpoint CIDR on port 1433 only from pods matching `podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: ingest } }`. That label comes from the security runbook template he's working off of -- an internal reference doc written months earlier, before grain-ingest's Helm chart existed, using the service's working name at the time. Nobody cross-checks it against the Deployment's actual `app: grain-ingest` label, because there's no obvious reason to: the policy and the Deployment are owned by the same engineer, reviewed in the same week, and feel like one unit of work even though they're applied through two completely different paths -- one through `helm upgrade`, one through a direct `kubectl apply -f`.

Dante validates the policy the way it's reasonable to validate a NetworkPolicy in isolation: he spins up a disposable test pod, hand-labels it `app: ingest` to match the rule he just wrote, confirms it can reach Azure SQL on 1433, then relabels it to something unrelated and confirms the connection is now blocked. Both results are exactly what he expects, so he signs off and merges the change into the security runbook as verified. What that test never does is connect to the database from an actual running `grain-ingest` pod -- the ones Lesson 9 deployed, carrying `app: grain-ingest`, not `app: ingest`. The policy passes every test it was given. It simply was never given the one test that would have caught this.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Confirm the gap in a pre-harvest security review

```
SECURITY REVIEW NOTE (Fairmont, pre-harvest):
  Any pod in the 'fairmont' namespace can currently reach Azure SQL's
  private endpoint directly. Only grain-ingest should be able to.
  Action: restrict DB egress to the ingestion service's pods only,
  before harvest traffic ramps up.
```

## Step 2 -- Write the default-deny baseline

```yaml
# networkpolicy-default-deny.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: fairmont
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector: {}
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
```

Everything loses default egress except DNS, which every workload still needs.

## Step 3 -- Write the allow rule for database access

```yaml
# networkpolicy-allow-db-ingest.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-db-ingest
  namespace: fairmont
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ingest
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: 10.20.4.0/24   # Azure SQL private endpoint subnet
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 1433
```

`app: ingest` comes straight out of the security runbook template this policy is based on -- written before the Helm chart existed, under the service's earlier working name. It is never diffed against `charts/grain-ingest/templates/deployment.yaml`.

## Step 4 -- Apply directly, outside the Helm chart

```bash
kubectl apply -f networkpolicy-default-deny.yaml
kubectl apply -f networkpolicy-allow-db-ingest.yaml
```

```
DANTE:  I'll fold both of these into the Helm chart as a proper
        templates/networkpolicy.yaml once the harvest freeze lifts --
        the review queue for chart changes is backed up a day, and
        this closes a real gap today instead of next week.
```

## Step 5 -- Validate the policy's logic with a disposable test pod

```bash
kubectl run netpol-test --image=nicolaka/netshoot -n fairmont \
  --labels="app=ingest" --restart=Never -- sleep 3600

kubectl exec -it netpol-test -n fairmont -- \
  nc -zv fairmont-sql.database.windows.net 1433
# Connection succeeds -- matches the rule, as expected.

kubectl label pod netpol-test -n fairmont app=other-service --overwrite
kubectl exec -it netpol-test -n fairmont -- \
  nc -zv fairmont-sql.database.windows.net 1433
# Connection times out -- correctly blocked.

kubectl delete pod netpol-test -n fairmont
```

Both outcomes are exactly what the policy is designed to do, so Dante signs it off.

## Step 6 -- Document it as closed

```
SECURITY REVIEW NOTE -- UPDATE:
  allow-db-ingest NetworkPolicy applied to 'fairmont' namespace.
  Verified: pods labeled app=ingest can reach Azure SQL on 1433;
  unlabeled/other pods cannot. Gap closed.
```

The verification is real and the policy behaves exactly as written. No step in this lesson ever points a connection test at a pod the Deployment actually created -- that comparison doesn't happen until much later in this project, when it matters.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Applied a default-deny-egress NetworkPolicy plus a narrow allow rule scoping Azure SQL access (port 1433) to podSelector app=ingest, directly via kubectl ahead of the Helm chart review cycle. Validated using a hand-labeled test pod, confirmed allow/deny behavior correctly -- but never cross-checked podSelector against the Deployment's actual app=grain-ingest label.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Closed a real pre-harvest security gap this week rather than waiting on next week's chart review -- only the ingestion service can now reach the database at the network layer. Tested and confirmed working.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We closed a security gap ahead of harvest that would have let any workload on the cluster reach the grain database directly. The fix is in place and was tested and verified before the season ramped up.

lessons.title: Identity and Access Hardening Across Azure and AWS
lessons.summary: Dante replaces stored credentials with least-privilege, managed identities on both clouds Fairmont touches: Azure AD Workload Identity for grain-ingest's Azure SQL access, and an IAM role for the legacy settlement-export job running on AWS.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Two separate credential problems have been sitting on Dante's backlog since before this project started. On Azure, grain-ingest connects to Azure SQL using a SQL login and password stored as a Kubernetes Secret -- functional, but a long-lived shared secret that has to be rotated by hand and that every pod in the chart can see in its environment. On AWS, Fairmont's older nightly settlement-export job -- an EC2 instance that uploads a daily co-op payout file to S3 for the accounting team -- authenticates with a long-lived IAM access key pasted into a config file years ago, never rotated since.

This lesson replaces both with identity, not secrets: Azure AD Workload Identity federates grain-ingest's Kubernetes service account directly to an Azure AD identity scoped to exactly the database role it needs, and an IAM role attached to the EC2 instance profile replaces the static AWS key, scoped to exactly the one S3 prefix the export job writes to. Nothing else about either workload's logic changes.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine two employees each carrying an old-fashioned physical key that opens one specific door, and that key gets copied and handed down to whoever has the job next, never changed. If a copy gets lost, you don't know who still has one, and the only fix is re-keying the whole lock.

This lesson swaps both of those old keys for a smarter badge system instead -- one for the Azure side, one for the AWS side. Each badge is tied to the specific worker, not copied and handed around, and each one only opens the one door that worker actually needs -- the grain data door, or the settlement-report door -- nothing else in the building. If someone leaves the job, their badge just stops working. Nobody has to go find and destroy a key.
lessons.explainProfessional:
On Azure, Dante sets up Azure AD Workload Identity: an Azure AD application registration (a user-assigned managed identity) gets a federated credential trusting the `fairmont` namespace's `grain-ingest` Kubernetes service account specifically, so AKS's workload identity webhook injects a short-lived, auto-rotated token into the pod rather than anything Dante has to manage. Inside Azure SQL, a contained database user is created `FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER` mapped to that same identity, and granted `db_datareader` and `db_datawriter` only -- no `db_owner`, no server-level role, nothing beyond what grain-ingest's own write path actually touches. The Kubernetes Secret holding the old SQL login is deleted once the cutover is confirmed, not left behind 'just in case.'

On AWS, the same principle applies to a much older piece of Fairmont's footprint: an IAM role with a trust policy scoped to the EC2 service, attached to the settlement-export instance via an instance profile, carrying a policy that permits `s3:PutObject` on exactly `arn:aws:s3:::fairmont-settlements/exports/*` and nothing else -- not the whole bucket, not any other bucket in the account. The export script is updated to drop its explicit `aws_access_key_id`/`aws_secret_access_key` entirely and let the AWS SDK pick up instance-profile credentials automatically. Both changes follow the identical shape: stop handing a workload a secret it has to keep safe, and instead give it an identity scoped to exactly the one thing it's allowed to do.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Audit what's actually in use today

```
CREDENTIAL AUDIT:
  grain-ingest (AKS)      -> SQL login/password, stored as a
                             Kubernetes Secret, manually rotated
  settlement-export (EC2) -> static AWS access key + secret,
                             pasted into config.ini, never rotated
```

## Step 2 (Azure) -- Create the managed identity and federate it

```bash
az identity create -g fairmont-rg -n grain-ingest-identity

az identity federated-credential create \
  --name grain-ingest-fedcred \
  --identity-name grain-ingest-identity \
  --resource-group fairmont-rg \
  --issuer "$(az aks show -g fairmont-rg -n fairmont-aks --query oidcIssuerProfile.issuerUrl -o tsv)" \
  --subject system:serviceaccount:fairmont:grain-ingest \
  --audience api://AzureADTokenExchange
```

## Step 3 -- Annotate the Kubernetes service account

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/serviceaccount.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
  namespace: fairmont
  annotations:
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "{{ .Values.managedIdentity.clientId }}"
  labels:
    azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
```

```yaml
# deployment.yaml -- pod template additions
spec:
  serviceAccountName: grain-ingest
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: grain-ingest
        azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
```

## Step 4 -- Scope the database role to least privilege

```sql
-- run against Fairmont's Azure SQL database
CREATE USER [grain-ingest-identity] FROM EXTERNAL PROVIDER;
ALTER ROLE db_datareader ADD MEMBER [grain-ingest-identity];
ALTER ROLE db_datawriter ADD MEMBER [grain-ingest-identity];
```

## Step 5 -- Remove the old secret once the cutover is confirmed

```bash
kubectl get pods -n fairmont -l app=grain-ingest   # confirm healthy
kubectl delete secret grain-ingest-sql-login -n fairmont
```

## Step 6 (AWS) -- Replace the settlement-export job's static key

```bash
aws iam create-role --role-name fairmont-settlement-export \
  --assume-role-policy-document file://ec2-trust-policy.json

aws iam put-role-policy --role-name fairmont-settlement-export \
  --policy-name settlement-export-s3-write \
  --policy-document '{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [{
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:PutObject",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::fairmont-settlements/exports/*"
    }]
  }'

aws iam create-instance-profile --instance-profile-name fairmont-settlement-export
aws iam add-role-to-instance-profile \
  --instance-profile-name fairmont-settlement-export \
  --role-name fairmont-settlement-export
aws ec2 associate-iam-instance-profile \
  --instance-id i-0abcd1234efgh5678 \
  --iam-instance-profile Name=fairmont-settlement-export
```

```ini
# config.ini -- before and after
# BEFORE: aws_access_key_id = AKIA...  (removed entirely)
# AFTER:  no credentials section -- SDK reads the instance profile
```

## Step 7 -- Validate both cutovers

Dante confirms grain-ingest's pods are writing to Azure SQL under the new identity with no application errors, and watches the next scheduled settlement export complete successfully against S3 with no key in the config file at all. Both workloads keep running exactly as before -- the only thing that changed is what they're allowed to do, and that nothing they use to prove who they are can be copied, leaked, or forgotten in a config file again.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Cut over grain-ingest from a stored SQL login to Azure AD Workload Identity (federated to the fairmont service account, scoped to db_datareader/db_datawriter only) and deleted the old Kubernetes Secret. On AWS, replaced the settlement-export job's static access key with an EC2 instance-profile IAM role scoped to a single S3 prefix. No application logic changed on either side.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Removed two long-standing credential risks -- a shared database password and an old AWS key nobody had rotated in years -- and replaced both with identities tied to the specific service that needs them, scoped to exactly what each one does. Both systems were validated end to end after the change.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We closed out two old security risks that had been sitting on the books: a shared database password and a years-old cloud access key. Both systems now authenticate with identity instead of a secret that could be copied or lost, and both were tested working after the change.

lessons.title: Automating Routine Ops with a Tag-Based Cleanup Script
lessons.summary: Dante writes a PowerShell runbook that finds untagged and orphaned Azure resources left behind by iteration -- unattached disks, stale public IPs -- and schedules it weekly through Azure Automation, closing out the routine-ops half of the build before harvest.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Weeks of iterating on the AKS cluster, Helm releases, and test pods have left Fairmont's Azure subscription with the usual residue: a handful of unattached managed disks from deleted PVCs, a public IP left over from an earlier load-balancer experiment, and a few resources that were never given Fairmont's standard tags at all. None of it is urgent, individually, but it's exactly the kind of drift that quietly inflates a cloud bill and that nobody notices until a FinOps review asks why costs don't match what's actually running.

This lesson builds the routine-ops fix: a PowerShell runbook, using Azure Resource Graph, that queries the subscription weekly for untagged resources and for disks sitting unattached, and reports them -- defaulting to a dry-run list, not automatic deletion. It runs on a schedule inside Azure Automation, under its own scoped managed identity, following the same least-privilege pattern as Lesson 11's identity work rather than a stored credential.
lessons.explainSimple:
Picture a self-storage facility doing a walk-through every Sunday morning, checking two things: which units don't have a name card on the door, and which units have been sitting completely empty with nobody renting them. The walkthrough doesn't throw anything away on its own -- it just writes down a list and hands it to the manager, because deciding what actually gets cleared out is a decision a person should make on purpose, not something that happens automatically in the background.

That's what this script does for Fairmont's cloud account. Every week, it quietly checks for cloud resources that either don't have the right label on them or aren't actually attached to anything useful anymore, and it hands someone a clean list -- instead of those things just sitting there, quietly costing money, until someone happens to notice months later.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The runbook authenticates with `Connect-AzAccount -Identity`, using the Azure Automation account's own system-assigned managed identity rather than a stored credential or service principal secret -- the same no-stored-secrets principle Lesson 11 applied to grain-ingest and the AWS export job, applied here to the automation tooling itself. That identity is granted `Reader` on the subscription plus a narrowly scoped custom role permitting `Microsoft.Compute/disks/delete` only, nothing broader.

The query itself runs through `Search-AzGraph`, using Azure Resource Graph's KQL-like query language rather than iterating resources one type at a time with `Get-AzResource` -- Resource Graph returns results across the whole subscription in one call and scales cleanly as Fairmont's footprint grows. Two checks run each week: resources missing any of Fairmont's three required tags (`cost-center`, `environment`, `owner`), and managed disks whose `diskState` is `Unattached` for longer than a seven-day grace window, which filters out disks mid-detach during a normal redeploy. Both reports land as a dry-run summary; nothing is deleted automatically. Deletion requires a second, explicit run of the script with a `-Confirm` switch, reviewed by Dante or whoever's on ops that week -- the automation's job is to surface drift reliably every week, not to make irreversible decisions unsupervised.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Define Fairmont's tagging policy

```
REQUIRED TAGS (every resource):
  cost-center   e.g. "grain-ops"
  environment   dev | staging | prod
  owner         the engineer or team responsible
```

## Step 2 -- Create the Automation Account's managed identity and scope it

```bash
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <automation-account-principal-id> \
  --role "Reader" \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub-id>

az role definition create --role-definition '{
  "Name": "Fairmont Disk Cleanup",
  "Actions": ["Microsoft.Compute/disks/delete"],
  "AssignableScopes": ["/subscriptions/<sub-id>"]
}'
```

## Step 3 -- Write the PowerShell runbook

```powershell
# Fairmont-WeeklyResourceCleanup.ps1
Connect-AzAccount -Identity

$requiredTags = @("cost-center", "environment", "owner")

# Find resources missing any required tag
$untagged = Search-AzGraph -Query @"
Resources
| extend tagKeys = bag_keys(tags)
| where not(array_length(set_intersection(tagKeys, dynamic(['cost-center','environment','owner']))) == 3)
| project name, type, resourceGroup, tagKeys
"@

# Find disks unattached for 7+ days
$cutoff = (Get-Date).AddDays(-7)
$orphanedDisks = Get-AzDisk | Where-Object {
    $_.DiskState -eq "Unattached" -and $_.TimeCreated -lt $cutoff
}

$report = [PSCustomObject]@{
    RunDate         = Get-Date -Format "yyyy-MM-dd"
    UntaggedCount   = $untagged.Count
    Untagged        = $untagged
    OrphanedDisks   = $orphanedDisks | Select-Object Name, ResourceGroupName, TimeCreated
}

$report | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 | Out-File "cleanup-report-$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd).json"
Write-Output "Found $($untagged.Count) untagged resources and $($orphanedDisks.Count) orphaned disks."
```

## Step 4 -- Dry run first, every time

By default the script only reports. Deletion is a deliberate, separate second step:

```powershell
param([switch]$Confirm)

if ($Confirm) {
    foreach ($disk in $orphanedDisks) {
        Remove-AzDisk -ResourceGroupName $disk.ResourceGroupName -DiskName $disk.Name -Force
        Write-Output "Deleted orphaned disk: $($disk.Name)"
    }
} else {
    Write-Output "Dry run only -- re-run with -Confirm to delete listed disks."
}
```

## Step 5 -- Schedule it weekly in Azure Automation

```bash
az automation schedule create \
  --automation-account-name fairmont-automation \
  --resource-group fairmont-rg \
  --name weekly-cleanup-schedule \
  --frequency Week --interval 1 --start-time "2026-11-02T06:00:00Z"

az automation job schedule create \
  --automation-account-name fairmont-automation \
  --resource-group fairmont-rg \
  --runbook-name Fairmont-WeeklyResourceCleanup \
  --schedule-name weekly-cleanup-schedule
```

## Step 6 -- Review the first report

The first run turns up two leftover unattached disks from earlier Helm chart testing and one untagged public IP from a load-balancer experiment weeks back. Dante tags the IP, confirms the two disks are genuinely unused, and runs the script a second time with `-Confirm` to remove them -- a small, routine cleanup that would otherwise have sat quietly on the bill until someone asked why.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Built a PowerShell runbook on Search-AzGraph that reports untagged resources and disks unattached 7+ days, authenticating via the Automation Account's own managed identity scoped to Reader plus a narrow disk-delete role. Runs weekly dry-run by default; deletion requires an explicit -Confirm pass. First run found two orphaned test disks and one untagged public IP.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: We now automatically catch leftover cloud resources from testing and iteration every week instead of relying on someone noticing an inflated bill later. The script reports first and only deletes anything when someone deliberately confirms it.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We put a routine weekly check in place that catches unused or untracked cloud resources before they quietly add up on the bill. Nothing gets deleted automatically -- it's flagged for review first, which is exactly the kind of cost discipline a FinOps review should find already in place.

lessons.title: Building the CI/CD Pipeline: Lint, Test, and Deploy the Helm Chart on Merge
lessons.summary: A GitOps-flavored pipeline -- lint the Helm chart, plan the Terraform, deploy on merge to main -- so Terraform, Docker/Kubernetes, and Git finally operate as one reviewable path instead of three disconnected manual steps.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
`grain-ingest` already runs on AKS as an HPA-autoscaled Deployment, deployed with Helm (Lesson 9), on top of infrastructure Terraform provisions with remote state locked in Azure Storage via blob leases. What doesn't exist yet is a pipeline that ties those three things -- Terraform, the Helm chart, and Git -- into one path everyone actually uses. Today, a change to `grain-ingest` means someone runs `terraform apply` from their laptop, then `helm upgrade` from their laptop, by hand, in whatever order they remember. That's exactly the kind of gap that let Lesson 10's NetworkPolicy get applied straight from a laptop with `kubectl apply`, completely out of band from the Helm chart that owns the Deployment it's supposed to protect -- nobody reviewed it next to the thing it selects.

This lesson closes that gap with a GitOps-flavored CI/CD pipeline in GitHub Actions: every pull request against the `grain-ingest` chart or its Terraform gets linted, templated, and plan-checked automatically, and a merge to `main` is the only thing that actually touches the cluster. Nothing about this pipeline knows about the label mismatch yet -- that's still sitting live in the cluster, undetected, and stays that way until the harvest incident two phases from now. But the pipeline this lesson builds is exactly the one Lesson 16 reaches for to make sure that mistake can never ship silently again.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a school science fair where students used to just walk their project straight to the gym floor and set it up themselves, with nobody checking it first. Sometimes two students' projects would end up wired together wrong without anyone noticing, because nobody ever looked at both projects side by side before they went on the floor.

This lesson builds a check-in table at the gym door. Every project has to stop there first -- a teacher looks it over, checks it against the rules, and only the projects that pass get carried onto the floor. Nobody sets anything up directly anymore; everything goes through the check-in table, every single time. That's what we're building for grain-ingest: a check-in table (the pipeline) that every change has to pass through before it ever touches the real cluster.
lessons.explainProfessional:
GitOps, at its narrowest and most useful definition, is the discipline that the only path to a running change is through a pull request that machines validate -- never a human running a command against production from a laptop. This lesson builds that path for `grain-ingest` specifically: a GitHub Actions workflow with a `validate` job that runs on every pull request (`helm lint` against the chart, `helm template` piped into a schema check, and `terraform plan` against the remote state in Azure Storage) and a `deploy` job gated to `on: push: branches: [main]` that runs `terraform apply` followed by `helm upgrade --install`, in that fixed order, so infrastructure always lands before the workload that depends on it.

The detail worth sitting with is what this pipeline does *not* yet check: it lints the Helm chart's syntax and validates it renders a schema-valid Kubernetes manifest, but it has no opinion yet about whether a Deployment's pod labels agree with a NetworkPolicy's `podSelector` -- because, as of this lesson, the NetworkPolicy from Lesson 10 isn't even part of this chart. It was applied directly with `kubectl apply`, so this brand-new pipeline has literally never seen it, lints it, or plans against it. That's not a flaw in this lesson's pipeline; it's the precise shape of the gap this pipeline exists to eventually close, once Lesson 16 pulls that NetworkPolicy in under the same roof.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Lay out the repo the pipeline will validate

```
grain-ingest/
  charts/
    grain-ingest/
      Chart.yaml
      values.yaml
      templates/
        deployment.yaml      # app: grain-ingest (Lesson 9)
        service.yaml
        hpa.yaml
  infra/
    main.tf                  # AKS, Azure SQL, remote state backend
    backend.tf                # azurerm backend, blob-lease locking
  .github/
    workflows/
      deploy.yml
```

Note what's conspicuously absent: `templates/networkpolicy.yaml`. Lesson 10's NetworkPolicy lives only as something someone ran `kubectl apply -f` against the cluster directly -- it has no file in this repo at all yet. This pipeline cannot lint, test, or plan something it was never shown.

## Step 2 -- Write the validate job (runs on every pull request)

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: grain-ingest-ci-cd
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["charts/grain-ingest/**", "infra/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["charts/grain-ingest/**", "infra/**"]

jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/setup-helm@v4
        with: { version: "3.14.0" }
      - name: Helm lint
        run: helm lint charts/grain-ingest
      - name: Render and schema-check the chart
        run: |
          helm template grain-ingest charts/grain-ingest > rendered.yaml
          helm template grain-ingest charts/grain-ingest | kubeconform -strict
      - name: Terraform init + plan
        working-directory: infra
        run: |
          terraform init -backend-config="key=grain-ingest.tfstate"
          terraform plan -out=tfplan
```

`kubeconform -strict` catches a Kubernetes manifest that's malformed or uses a field that doesn't exist on that API version -- it has no concept of whether two *different* manifests' label selectors agree with each other, because today's rendered output only contains the Deployment, Service, and HPA. There's nothing in this render for a label mismatch to even hide in yet.

## Step 3 -- Write the deploy job (runs only after merge to `main`)

```yaml
  deploy:
    needs: validate
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: azure/login@v2
        with: { creds: ${{ secrets.AZURE_CREDENTIALS }} }
      - name: Terraform apply
        working-directory: infra
        run: |
          terraform init -backend-config="key=grain-ingest.tfstate"
          terraform apply -auto-approve
      - uses: azure/setup-helm@v4
        with: { version: "3.14.0" }
      - name: Deploy grain-ingest via Helm
        run: |
          az aks get-credentials --resource-group fairmont-grain-rg --name fairmont-grain-aks
          helm upgrade --install grain-ingest charts/grain-ingest \
            --namespace grain --create-namespace \
            --atomic --timeout 5m
```

`environment: production` with a required reviewer on that GitHub Environment is what makes this a real gate, not a formality -- a merge to `main` still needs one human to click approve before `deploy` runs, which is the GitOps middle ground between "anyone can kubectl apply anything" and "no human ever looks at a production change."

## Step 4 -- Confirm the remote state lock actually prevents a concurrent apply

```hcl
# infra/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "azurerm" {
    resource_group_name  = "fairmont-grain-rg"
    storage_account_name = "fairmontgrainstate"
    container_name        = "tfstate"
    key                    = "grain-ingest.tfstate"
  }
}
```

Azure Storage's blob-lease locking means a second `terraform apply` -- say, someone running one from a laptop out of habit, right as this pipeline's `deploy` job is mid-run -- gets a clear `Error: Error acquiring the state lock` instead of silently racing the pipeline and corrupting state. Test this deliberately once: kick off the pipeline, then try `terraform apply` locally against the same backend, and confirm it blocks rather than proceeds.

## Step 5 -- Open a real pull request and watch the gate work

Change `replicaCount` in `values.yaml`, open a PR, and confirm `validate` runs and passes, `deploy` does not run (wrong branch), and merging to `main` triggers `deploy`, pauses on the `production` environment's required reviewer, and only then runs `terraform apply` and `helm upgrade`.

## Step 6 -- Write down what this pipeline does and doesn't guard against yet

```
THIS PIPELINE CATCHES:
  - Malformed Helm chart syntax (helm lint)
  - A rendered manifest that violates the Kubernetes API schema (kubeconform)
  - A Terraform plan that would fail or drift unexpectedly
  - Two people applying infra changes at the same time (state lock)

THIS PIPELINE DOES NOT YET CATCH:
  - Any resource applied to the cluster OUTSIDE this repo and this
    pipeline (kubectl apply run by hand -- exactly how Lesson 10's
    NetworkPolicy got onto the cluster)
  - Two manifests whose label selectors silently disagree with each
    other, because nothing in this chart defines more than one
    label-selecting resource yet
```

That second list isn't a gap to panic over today -- it's a gap worth writing down plainly, because it's exactly the gap the harvest incident later in this series walks straight into.

workplaceExplanation.technicalLead: Stood up a GitHub Actions pipeline for grain-ingest: a validate job on every PR (helm lint, kubeconform schema check against the rendered chart, terraform plan) and a deploy job gated to main with a required environment reviewer, running terraform apply then helm upgrade in that order. Remote state in Azure Storage with blob-lease locking confirmed to block a concurrent apply. Flagged explicitly that this pipeline has no visibility into anything applied outside it -- including Lesson 10's NetworkPolicy, which still lives only as a manual kubectl apply.
workplaceExplanation.projectManager: Every future change to the ingestion service now goes through one reviewed, automated path instead of someone running commands from their laptop by hand. A merge still needs a human to approve the deploy step, so we have both automation and a real checkpoint.
workplaceExplanation.executive: Changes to the grain ingestion system now go through an automatic review-and-deploy process instead of relying on someone remembering the right manual steps in the right order. That's a reliability improvement on its own, and it's also the foundation we'll build on when we tighten this further later in the project.

lessons.title: Setting Azure Cost Budgets and Finishing the Reliability Dashboard
lessons.summary: An Azure Cost Management budget and anomaly alert scoped to the grain-ingest resource group, plus the pod-cost-versus-database-load panel added to the reliability dashboard from Lesson 7 -- the exact view that will surface the harvest incident two lessons from now.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
The reliability dashboard Dante Okafor first stood up back in Lesson 7 already tracks the basics for `grain-ingest`: pod count, HPA replica trend, request latency. What it's never had is a cost lens or an explicit pairing against the one downstream resource `grain-ingest` actually exists to feed -- Azure SQL. This lesson adds both. First, an Azure Cost Management budget scoped to the `fairmont-grain-rg` resource group, provisioned through the same Terraform this series has used for everything else, with an action group that emails and pages on an actual anomaly, not just a static threshold. Second, a new panel on the existing dashboard that plots AKS pod count and estimated compute cost side by side with Azure SQL DTU percentage for the same time window.

Neither half of this lesson is built with the harvest incident in mind -- as far as anyone at Fairmont Grain Co-op knows right now, this is routine FinOps and reliability hygiene, the kind every well-run platform has. But this exact pod-cost-vs-DTU panel is the only reason anyone catches what happens during harvest: it's the one place on the entire platform where "the autoscaler did its job correctly" and "the database never heard about it" would visibly contradict each other, and right now there is no other instrument on this platform that would show that contradiction at all.
lessons.explainSimple:
Think about a car's dashboard that shows both the speedometer and the fuel gauge. If you're pressing the gas pedal harder and the speedometer climbs, you'd expect the fuel gauge to drop faster too -- they should move together. If the speedometer says you're going 70 but the fuel gauge hasn't moved in twenty minutes, something is wrong with the car, even though neither gauge on its own looks broken.

That's the new dial we're adding today. One gauge shows how many extra workers (pods) got hired and how much that's costing. The other gauge shows how hard the database is actually working. Normally, when more workers get hired, the database should get busier too, because that's the whole point of hiring them. Putting both gauges on the same dashboard means if one ever climbs while the other doesn't, it's visible immediately -- instead of each gauge quietly looking fine all by itself.
lessons.explainProfessional:
This lesson deliberately treats cost and reliability as the same instrumentation problem, which is the core idea FinOps brings to a platform like this one: cost is a leading indicator of behavior, not just a line item to review monthly. The Azure Cost Management budget (`azurerm_consumption_budget_resource_group`, scoped to `fairmont-grain-rg`, with a 90% and 100%-of-forecast anomaly threshold tied to an action group) gives Fairmont's finance side the alerting it actually asked for. But the more consequential addition is architectural: a new Azure Monitor Workbook panel that runs a KQL query joining `ContainerInventory`/`InsightsMetrics` (AKS pod count and estimated node-hour cost) against `AzureMetrics` for the Azure SQL `dtu_consumption_percent` metric, both bucketed to the same 5-minute window, plotted on shared time axes.

The reason this specific pairing matters, and the reason it's worth building now rather than treating it as a nice-to-have: `grain-ingest`'s entire job is writing scanned grain-elevator telemetry into Azure SQL, so under any correctly functioning autoscale event, pod count rising should correlate with DTU usage rising within a short lag -- more workers writing more rows. A world where pod count and cost climb while DTU stays flat or falls is not a state this system should ever be in during normal operation, and as of this lesson, it is the *only* signal on the entire platform that would catch that state, because no alert anywhere is wired to "a pod can't reach its database" directly -- only to a pod crashing, which, as this series' incident shows two lessons from now, is not what happens when a NetworkPolicy silently blocks egress.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Provision the Cost Management budget in Terraform

```hcl
# infra/cost_management.tf
resource "azurerm_monitor_action_group" "finops_alerts" {
  name                = "grain-ingest-finops-ag"
  resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.grain.name
  short_name          = "grainfin"

  email_receiver {
    name          = "platform-oncall"
    email_address = "platform-oncall@fairmontgrain.example"
  }
}

resource "azurerm_consumption_budget_resource_group" "grain_ingest_budget" {
  name              = "grain-ingest-monthly-budget"
  resource_group_id = azurerm_resource_group.grain.id
  amount            = 4200
  time_grain        = "Monthly"

  time_period {
    start_date = "2026-10-01T00:00:00Z"
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 90
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.finops_alerts.id]
  }

  notification {
    enabled        = true
    threshold      = 100
    operator       = "GreaterThanOrEqualTo"
    threshold_type = "Forecasted"
    contact_groups = [azurerm_monitor_action_group.finops_alerts.id]
  }
}
```

The forecasted-100% notification is the one that actually behaves like an anomaly alert -- it fires on a trajectory, not just a number already crossed, which matters because harvest season's autoscale-driven spend ramps fast enough that a simple "already over budget" alert would land too late to act on.

## Step 2 -- Run it through Lesson 13's pipeline, not by hand

```
git checkout -b add-cost-management-budget
# add infra/cost_management.tf
git push && open a pull request
```

The `validate` job's `terraform plan` shows exactly what this adds before anyone merges -- the same gate every other infra change goes through now, cost tooling included.

## Step 3 -- Extend the Lesson 7 reliability dashboard with the paired KQL panel

```kql
// Azure Monitor Workbook panel: "Pod/Cost vs. Database Load"
let pods = InsightsMetrics
    | where Namespace == "container.azm.ms/kube-state"
    | where Name == "kube_pod_status_phase" and TimeGenerated > ago(6h)
    | where tostring(Tags.phase) == "Running"
    | where Tags.pod_name startswith "grain-ingest"
    | summarize running_pods = dcount(Tags.pod_name) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m);
let dtu = AzureMetrics
    | where ResourceId has "fairmont-grain-sql"
    | where MetricName == "dtu_consumption_percent" and TimeGenerated > ago(6h)
    | summarize avg_dtu = avg(Average) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m);
pods
| join kind=inner dtu on TimeGenerated
| project TimeGenerated, running_pods, avg_dtu
| render timechart
```

Plot `running_pods` and `avg_dtu` on the same chart, shared time axis. Under normal operation, the two lines should visibly track each other during any autoscale event -- that correlation, confirmed here under normal conditions, is exactly what Lesson 15 goes looking for and fails to find.

## Step 4 -- Add the estimated-cost series alongside pod count

```kql
let cost = InsightsMetrics
    | where Namespace == "container.azm.ms/kube-state"
    | where Name == "kube_node_status_capacity_cpu_cores" and TimeGenerated > ago(6h)
    | summarize estimated_hourly_cost = sum(Val) * 0.096 by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)  // AKS node-hour rate
```

Join this alongside the pod/DTU panel so the dashboard reads, left to right: pod count up, cost up, DTU up -- three lines that should move together. Label the panel plainly: "If cost and pod count rise without DTU rising, autoscaling worked but the database never heard about it."

## Step 5 -- Validate the panel against a known-good autoscale event

Trigger a small synthetic load burst against `grain-ingest` (a short `k6` run is enough), watch the HPA scale replicas up, and confirm all three lines -- pods, cost, DTU -- rise together within a few minutes on the dashboard. Screenshot this known-good correlation and keep it; it's the baseline Lesson 15 compares the harvest incident against.

## Step 6 -- Set a dashboard alert on the divergence itself, not just on the budget

```kql
// Alert rule: pod count rising, DTU flat or falling, sustained 10+ minutes
pods
| join kind=inner dtu on TimeGenerated
| extend pod_delta = running_pods - prev(running_pods, 1)
| extend dtu_delta = avg_dtu - prev(avg_dtu, 1)
| where pod_delta > 0 and dtu_delta <= 0
| summarize divergent_windows = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where divergent_windows >= 2
```

Wire this as a scheduled Azure Monitor alert rule on the same action group from Step 1. As of this lesson it's untested against a real incident -- that test arrives, unplanned, during harvest.

lessons.title: Grain Elevators Went Quiet: Finding the Gap Between Cost and Database Load
lessons.summary: During peak harvest, the reliability dashboard shows pod count and cost climbing exactly as the HPA intended -- while Azure SQL's DTU usage stays flat. No pod ever crashes. Dante's kubectl investigation narrows the silence to a one-word label mismatch between the Lesson 9 Deployment and the Lesson 10 NetworkPolicy.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
It's peak fall harvest at Fairmont Grain Co-op, and several grain elevators go quiet -- their scan data simply stops showing up anywhere downstream, for roughly 40 minutes, during the single busiest reporting window of the year. Nothing in the usual places says anything is wrong: no pod restarts, no crash-loop alert, no PagerDuty page. The only thing that moves is the Lesson 14 dashboard panel built for exactly this kind of situation -- pod count and estimated cost climbing cleanly, right on schedule with the harvest traffic spike, while Azure SQL's DTU percentage stays essentially flat. That mismatch, not an alert, is what gets Dante Okafor's attention.

This lesson follows that investigation in order: confirming the dashboard anomaly is real and not a graphing artifact, checking that HPA actually did its job (it did -- new pods exist, carrying the right labels), and then doing the thing that finally exposes the problem -- pulling the live Deployment and the live NetworkPolicy out of the cluster with `kubectl get -o yaml`, side by side, and finding that they've been describing two different sets of pods the entire time. Lesson 9's Helm chart labeled every `grain-ingest` pod `app: grain-ingest`. Lesson 10's NetworkPolicy, applied straight to the cluster out of band from that same chart, selects `app: ingest` -- one word off, and silently wrong since the day it was applied.
lessons.explainSimple:
Imagine a security guard at a school who was told to only let kids wearing a "7th Grade" wristband through a certain door. But somebody printed this year's wristbands saying "Grade 7" instead of "7th Grade." Every single 7th grader gets stopped at the door, every day, and nobody notices for weeks, because the kids don't scream or make a scene -- they just quietly stand there, confused, and eventually wander off. No alarm goes off, because nothing "broke." The guard is doing exactly what he was told; the wristbands are exactly what the printer made. They just don't match each other.

That's exactly what happened at Fairmont Grain during harvest. New worker pods got created correctly, with the right job to do. A separate rule, written weeks earlier, was supposed to let those exact workers talk to the database -- but it was looking for a slightly different name tag than the one the workers were actually wearing. So the workers existed, were doing their job, and just quietly couldn't get through the door to the database. Nothing crashed, so nothing screamed for help. The only reason anyone noticed is that someone was watching a totally different gauge -- cost going up while database activity stayed flat -- and that mismatch is what gave the whole thing away.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The investigative discipline here is the same one this program has taught before: when something silently fails without crashing, the alerting you already have is, by definition, the wrong instrument -- you have to go find the signal that would actually catch this specific failure mode, and the Lesson 14 pod-cost-vs-DTU panel is exactly that signal. Confirming the HPA genuinely scaled correctly is the first move, not an afterthought: `kubectl get hpa grain-ingest -n grain` and `kubectl get pods -l app=grain-ingest -n grain` both show the expected new replicas, with the expected `app: grain-ingest` label, running and Ready. That rules out the easy, wrong explanations fast -- this isn't a crash loop, isn't a scheduling failure, and isn't the autoscaler malfunctioning.

What actually isolates the cause is comparing two live cluster objects that were never meant to diverge: `kubectl get deployment grain-ingest -n grain -o yaml` shows `spec.selector.matchLabels.app: grain-ingest`, exactly as Lesson 9's Helm chart wrote it. `kubectl get networkpolicy -n grain -o yaml` shows `spec.podSelector.matchLabels.app: ingest` on the NetworkPolicy Lesson 10 applied directly to the cluster, out of band from that same Helm chart. Those are two different selector values, and Kubernetes NetworkPolicy selection is exact-match, not fuzzy -- a pod labeled `app: grain-ingest` simply does not match a `podSelector` of `app: ingest`, full stop. Every pod the HPA created during harvest, old and new alike, has silently never matched this policy; existing long-running pods may have been grandfathered in under a looser historical rule or simply never restarted since before the policy was tightened, but any pod freshly created by the autoscaler during this exact harvest spike inherits the mismatch immediately, with TCP connections to Azure SQL timing out and retrying -- never crashing, never alerting, just quietly going nowhere for roughly 40 minutes of peak reporting.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Start from the dashboard, because nothing else fired

```
Fairmont Grain Co-op -- Reliability Dashboard (Lesson 14 panel)
Time window: harvest peak, 2026-10-xx 13:40 - 14:25

running_pods:     6 -> 14 (HPA scaled up, as designed)
estimated_cost:   rising in step with running_pods, as expected
avg_dtu:          holding flat at ~18%, no increase at all
```

No PagerDuty alert. No pod restart count above zero. The only signal anywhere on the platform is this one chart, and it's a correlation that *stopped* holding, not an alert that fired.

## Step 2 -- Rule out the obvious, wrong explanations first

```bash
kubectl get hpa grain-ingest -n grain
# NAME           REFERENCE                 TARGETS   MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
# grain-ingest   Deployment/grain-ingest   78%/70%   3         20        14

kubectl get pods -n grain -l app=grain-ingest
# NAME                           READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# grain-ingest-7f8d9c-k2p4q       1/1     Running   0          6m
# grain-ingest-7f8d9c-m9x1z       1/1     Running   0          6m
# ... (14 pods total, all Running, 0 restarts)
```

The HPA scaled correctly and every new pod is `Running` with zero restarts and the correct `app: grain-ingest` label. This confirms the failure is not a crash, not a scheduling problem, and not the autoscaler -- which also explains, precisely, why no existing alert fired. Every alert on this platform is wired to a pod *failing*, and these pods never fail.

## Step 3 -- Confirm the symptom directly: can a new pod actually reach the database?

```bash
kubectl exec -n grain grain-ingest-7f8d9c-k2p4q -- \
  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 telnet://fairmont-grain-sql.database.windows.net:1433
# * Trying 20.42.x.x:1433...
# * connect to 20.42.x.x port 1433 failed: Connection timed out
```

Connection timeout, not connection refused -- that distinction matters. A refused connection usually means the database rejected the client; a silent timeout on an internal cluster egress path is the signature of a NetworkPolicy quietly dropping the traffic rather than the destination ever seeing it.

## Step 4 -- Pull the Deployment and the NetworkPolicy side by side

```bash
kubectl get deployment grain-ingest -n grain -o yaml
```
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: grain-ingest        # from Lesson 9's Helm chart
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: grain-ingest       # every pod this Deployment creates gets this
```
```bash
kubectl get networkpolicy -n grain -o yaml
```
```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest-allow-sql
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ingest               # from Lesson 10's out-of-band kubectl apply
  policyTypes: [Egress]
  egress:
    - to: [{ ipBlock: { cidr: "20.42.0.0/16" } }]
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 1433 }]
```

There it is: `app: grain-ingest` versus `app: ingest`. Every pod this Deployment has ever created carries a label this NetworkPolicy's selector has never actually matched.

## Step 5 -- Confirm the mismatch, don't just eyeball it

```bash
kubectl get pods -n grain -l app=ingest
# No resources found in grain namespace.

kubectl get pods -n grain -l app=grain-ingest --no-headers | wc -l
# 14
```

Zero pods match the NetworkPolicy's selector. Fourteen pods match the Deployment's. This policy has been selecting nothing, for every pod that currently exists, this entire time.

## Step 6 -- Explain why this specific incident surfaced only now, during harvest

```
TIMELINE RECONSTRUCTED:
  Lesson 9:  Helm deploys grain-ingest, pods labeled app: grain-ingest.
  Lesson 10: NetworkPolicy applied out-of-band, podSelector app: ingest.
             -- mismatch introduced here, silently, no alert possible.
  Since then: baseline traffic (3-6 pods) apparently still got through --
             worth checking whether a broader historical allow rule or
             node-level NSG was masking this for steady-state load.
  Harvest:   HPA scales 6 -> 14 pods under real traffic. Every pod the
             autoscaler creates inherits app: grain-ingest and the same
             mismatch. At steady low traffic the gap may have been small
             enough to miss; at harvest volume, ~40 minutes of missing
             telemetry from several elevators became impossible to miss.
```

## Step 7 -- Write down exactly what's proven before opening the chart to fix it

```
PROVEN: HPA scaled grain-ingest correctly, 6 -> 14 pods, all Running, 0 restarts.
PROVEN: New pods cannot reach Azure SQL -- connection times out, not refused.
PROVEN: The Deployment's pod label (app: grain-ingest) and the NetworkPolicy's
        podSelector (app: ingest) are a one-word mismatch -- zero pods ever
        matched this policy.
PROVEN: This is a silent connectivity gap, not a crash -- which is exactly
        why no existing alert fired, and why only the Lesson 14 cost/DTU
        panel caught it at all.
NOT YET FIXED: the YAML itself, a way to stop this specific mismatch from
        ever shipping again, and a way to catch the next connectivity gap
        that doesn't involve a crash either.
```

Lesson 16 opens the chart next, with this exact diagnosis in hand.

Confirmed via kubectl get deployment/networkpolicy -o yaml side by side and kubectl get pods -l app=ingest returning zero matches. HPA scaled correctly (6 to 14 pods, all Running, 0 restarts) -- the failure is egress to Azure SQL timing out silently, never a crash, which is why no existing alert fired. Caught only because the Lesson 14 pod-cost-vs-DTU dashboard panel showed cost climbing while DTU stayed flat.

The system never crashed, which is exactly why normal alerts missed it -- we caught it because a cost dashboard we'd built for a different reason happened to show something didn't add up. Fix is scoped next.
workplaceExplanation.executive: We've identified exactly why some grain elevators' data went missing for about 40 minutes during harvest: a configuration mismatch between two settings that should have described the same thing but didn't, introduced silently weeks earlier. Nothing crashed, which is why it wasn't caught sooner -- it was caught because we'd already built a cost-monitoring view that happened to reveal the inconsistency. We know precisely what to fix.

lessons.title: Fixing the Label Mismatch and Proving Telemetry Flows End to End
lessons.summary: Merging the NetworkPolicy into the same Helm chart as the Deployment with the corrected selector, adding a CI check that fails any future pull request where the two disagree again, adding a real synthetic database health check, and validating all of it against a fresh autoscale event with zero telemetry gap.
lessons.whatAreWeBuilding:
Lesson 15 proved the exact mechanism: `grain-ingest`'s Deployment labels its pods `app: grain-ingest`; the NetworkPolicy Lesson 10 applied directly to the cluster, completely out of band from that Deployment's Helm chart, selects `app: ingest`. Two sources of truth -- a chart and a standalone `kubectl apply` -- silently diverged, and nothing on the platform was positioned to notice until the Lesson 14 dashboard did.

This lesson closes all three gaps that allowed it, not just the one YAML value. First, the NetworkPolicy moves into the same Helm chart as the Deployment, with its `podSelector` corrected to `app: grain-ingest`, so there is exactly one place that defines this pod's identity, never two. Second, Lesson 13's pipeline gets a new CI job that renders the chart and fails the pull request outright if a Deployment's pod labels and any NetworkPolicy's `podSelector` in the same chart ever disagree again -- the mistake becomes structurally impossible to merge, not just corrected once. Third, a real synthetic health check -- an actual periodic connection attempt to Azure SQL, not a liveness probe on the pod itself -- gets added to the monitoring stack, so an application-level connectivity gap triggers an alert directly, the next time, even if no pod ever crashes. The lesson closes by triggering a fresh autoscale event and confirming, on the same dashboard that caught the original problem, that telemetry now flows with zero gap end to end.
lessons.explainSimple:
Remember the mixed-up wristbands from last time -- "7th Grade" versus "Grade 7"? The real fix isn't just reprinting one wristband correctly. It's making sure the wristband printer and the door guard's instructions come from the exact same sheet of paper from now on, so they can never say two different things again. On top of that, we're adding a rule that checks, automatically, every single time new instructions get printed, that the wristband and the door guard's list still say the exact same thing -- before anyone's allowed to hand out the new wristbands at all. And just in case something else like this slips through anyway, we're also setting up a guard who walks over and personally tries the door every couple of minutes, instead of only reacting if a kid falls down and makes a scene.

Finally, we actually test it: we bring in a big new group of kids all at once (a fresh autoscale event) and watch, on the same gauge that caught the problem last time, that every single one of them gets through the door with nobody left standing outside confused.
lessons.explainProfessional:
The fix itself is small -- one line, `app: ingest` becomes `app: grain-ingest` -- which is exactly why it isn't the point of this lesson. The point is removing the structural condition that let a one-line mistake ship silently and persist undetected for weeks: two independently-maintained sources of truth describing the same pod's identity. Folding `templates/networkpolicy.yaml` into the same Helm chart as `templates/deployment.yaml`, and having both reference the same `{{ .Values.labels.app }}` value rather than two independently hand-typed strings, means there is no longer a second file for a reviewer to forget to open, and no deploy path that can apply one without the other.

The CI check matters more than the fix, because it's the piece that survives after everyone involved in this incident has moved on to other work: a small Python script parses the chart's rendered output, pulls every Deployment's `spec.selector.matchLabels` and every NetworkPolicy's `spec.podSelector.matchLabels` in the same render, and fails the pipeline if any NetworkPolicy's selector doesn't exactly match a Deployment's pod labels in that same chart. Wired into the `validate` job built in Lesson 13, this means Lesson 10's exact mistake -- a NetworkPolicy quietly selecting the wrong label -- cannot merge again, regardless of who makes it or how confident they are it's correct. The synthetic health check closes the remaining blind spot this incident exposed independent of the label bug specifically: a CronJob that attempts a real `SELECT 1` against Azure SQL on a tight interval and alerts on failure gives the platform an application-level signal for "can this service actually reach its database," which is a fundamentally different -- and in this case, the only relevant -- question from "is this pod's process still running," the thing every existing liveness probe and crash-loop alert was actually answering.
lessons.writtenInstructions:
## Step 1 -- Merge the NetworkPolicy into the same chart as the Deployment

```
charts/grain-ingest/
  Chart.yaml
  values.yaml
  templates/
    deployment.yaml
    service.yaml
    hpa.yaml
    networkpolicy.yaml        # NEW -- moved in from the standalone kubectl apply
```

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/values.yaml (add a single shared label value)
labels:
  app: grain-ingest
```

## Step 2 -- Template the Deployment's pod labels from that one value

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Values.labels.app }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: {{ .Values.labels.app }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: grain-ingest
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
```

## Step 3 -- Write the corrected NetworkPolicy, templated from the exact same value

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/networkpolicy.yaml  -- THE FIX
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest-allow-sql
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: {{ .Values.labels.app }}   # was hand-typed as "ingest" via kubectl apply;
                                        # now the SAME value the Deployment uses, always
  policyTypes:
    - Egress
  egress:
    - to:
        - ipBlock:
            cidr: {{ .Values.azureSqlCidr | quote }}
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 1433
```

Because both resources now read `{{ .Values.labels.app }}`, it is no longer possible for one of them to drift without the other changing too -- there's exactly one place to edit, and editing it updates both.

## Step 4 -- Remove the orphaned standalone policy and deploy through the pipeline, not by hand

```bash
kubectl delete networkpolicy grain-ingest-allow-sql -n grain   # the old, out-of-band one
git checkout -b fix-networkpolicy-label-mismatch
# add templates/networkpolicy.yaml, update values.yaml and deployment.yaml
git push && open a pull request
```

The old policy is deleted deliberately, by hand, once -- from this point forward, this resource's entire lifecycle belongs to the chart and Lesson 13's pipeline, never to a standalone `kubectl apply` again.

## Step 5 -- Add the CI label-match check to Lesson 13's validate job

```python
# ci/check_label_match.py
import sys, yaml

docs = list(yaml.safe_load_all(open(sys.argv[1])))
deployments = [d for d in docs if d and d.get("kind") == "Deployment"]
policies = [d for d in docs if d and d.get("kind") == "NetworkPolicy"]

failed = False
for dep in deployments:
    dep_labels = dep["spec"]["selector"]["matchLabels"]
    for pol in policies:
        pol_selector = pol["spec"].get("podSelector", {}).get("matchLabels", {})
        if not pol_selector:
            continue  # an empty selector intentionally means "all pods" -- not this bug
        if pol_selector != dep_labels:
            print(f"FAIL: NetworkPolicy '{pol['metadata']['name']}' podSelector "
                  f"{pol_selector} does not match Deployment '{dep['metadata']['name']}' "
                  f"pod labels {dep_labels}")
            failed = True

if failed:
    sys.exit(1)
print("OK: every NetworkPolicy podSelector matches its Deployment's pod labels")
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml -- new step inside the existing validate job
      - name: Check Deployment/NetworkPolicy label agreement
        run: |
          helm template grain-ingest charts/grain-ingest > rendered.yaml
          python3 ci/check_label_match.py rendered.yaml
```

This check is deliberately scoped to resources rendered *together*, in the same chart, on the same pull request -- it has no way to catch a NetworkPolicy applied directly with `kubectl` ever again, which is exactly why Step 4's cleanup, and never doing that again, matters as much as the script itself.

## Step 6 -- Prove the check actually fails on the original mistake

Before merging the fix, temporarily revert just the NetworkPolicy's label to `app: ingest` locally and rerun the check to confirm it's not a check that would have passed either way:

```bash
$ python3 ci/check_label_match.py rendered.yaml
FAIL: NetworkPolicy 'grain-ingest-allow-sql' podSelector {'app': 'ingest'} does not match Deployment 'grain-ingest' pod labels {'app': 'grain-ingest'}
```

Confirmed it catches the exact historical bug. Restore the corrected value and rerun -- it passes. Only then merge.

## Step 7 -- Add the real synthetic database health check

```yaml
# charts/grain-ingest/templates/db-healthcheck-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: grain-ingest-db-healthcheck
spec:
  schedule: "*/2 * * * *"
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        metadata:
          labels:
            app: {{ .Values.labels.app }}   # covered by the SAME NetworkPolicy, on purpose
        spec:
          containers:
            - name: db-healthcheck
              image: mcr.microsoft.com/mssql-tools
              env:
                - { name: SQL_SERVER, value: "fairmont-grain-sql.database.windows.net" }
              command: ["/bin/sh", "-c"]
              args:
                - >
                  sqlcmd -S $(SQL_SERVER) -d grain_telemetry -U $(SQL_USER) -P $(SQL_PASSWORD)
                  -Q "SELECT 1" -l 10 || exit 1
          restartPolicy: Never
```

Giving this CronJob's pods the exact same `app: {{ .Values.labels.app }}` label means it is itself subject to the same NetworkPolicy every real `grain-ingest` pod is -- so if this specific label mismatch (or any future one like it) ever recurs, this health check fails within two minutes, by design, instead of waiting for a customer-facing symptom.

## Step 8 -- Wire the health check's failure to an actual alert

```kql
// Azure Monitor alert rule on CronJob failure
KubePodInventory
| where Namespace == "grain"
| where Name startswith "grain-ingest-db-healthcheck"
| where PodStatus == "Failed"
| summarize failures = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where failures >= 1
```

Wire this to the same `finops_alerts` action group from Lesson 14 -- this is now the direct, application-level signal for "grain-ingest can't reach the database," independent of pod crash status entirely.

## Step 9 -- Validate with a fresh autoscale event, on the dashboard that caught the original bug

```bash
# trigger a load burst, same method used to validate Lesson 14's dashboard originally
k6 run --vus 200 --duration 5m grain-ingest-load-test.js
```

```
Fairmont Grain Co-op -- Reliability Dashboard, post-fix validation
running_pods:    6 -> 15 (HPA scales, as before)
estimated_cost:  rising in step with running_pods, as before
avg_dtu:         18% -> 54%, rising in step with pod count and cost -- MATCHES, this time
```

## Step 10 -- Confirm zero telemetry gap at the source, not just on the dashboard

```bash
kubectl exec -n grain grain-ingest-<new-pod> -- \
  curl -v --connect-timeout 5 telnet://fairmont-grain-sql.database.windows.net:1433
# * Connected to 20.42.x.x port 1433

kubectl logs -n grain grain-ingest-db-healthcheck-<latest> | tail -n 3
# 1
# (1 rows affected)
```

Every newly autoscaled pod reaches Azure SQL directly, and the synthetic health check passes throughout the load test. Close the loop the same way the harvest incident was found: by confirming the cost-vs-DTU panel, the service's own connectivity, and the new synthetic check all agree, this time -- then document the fix and the two new permanent safeguards in the incident record so the next engineer who touches this chart inherits the reasoning, not just the corrected YAML.

Added a CI job (ci/check_label_match.py) to Lesson 13's validate pipeline that fails any PR where a Deployment's pod labels and a NetworkPolicy's podSelector in the same chart disagree -- verified it actually catches the original app:ingest/app:grain-ingest mismatch before merging the fix. Added a CronJob synthetic DB health check (real SELECT 1 against Azure SQL every 2 minutes, same pod label, same NetworkPolicy) wired to an Azure Monitor alert, giving an application-level connectivity signal independent of pod crash status. Validated with a fresh k6-driven autoscale event: pod count, cost, and DTU now all rise together with zero connectivity gap.
